articles.title: Building Warrant: Every Agent-Made Change, Traced to the Human Who Said Yes
articles.description: How we built Warrant for the Flip the Switch Hackathon 2026—a deterministic scope gatekeeper and hash-linked authorization ledger for autonomous coding agents.
articles.body_html:
Built for the **Flip the Switch Hackathon 2026* (WeMakeDevs × DevTools Academy × Switch) — Track: Best Business Workflow.*

  • 🌐 Live Web App: https://warrant-web-ncno.onrender.com
  • ⚙️ Backend API & Swagger Docs: https://warrant-clerk.onrender.com/docs
  • 📦 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Shreyansh00987/Warrant
  • 🎬 1-Minute Demo Video: Watch on GitHub

1. The Dilemma of Autonomous Coding Agents

Engineering teams are in a rush to adopt autonomous coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode. These agents can read a Jira issue, explore a monorepo, refactor legacy code, and open pull requests in seconds.

But there is a glaring governance blind spot:
Human authorization currently lives scattered across private terminal windows and ephemeral direct messages.

When a pull request is approved on GitHub, all anyone knows is that a reviewer stamped a final git diff. Nobody can later answer:

  1. Who authorized this agent to make this change?
  2. What exact plan was approved?
  3. Did the agent stay strictly inside the authorized scope, or did it sneakily drift into sensitive files (like billing or auth)?

To solve this, we built Warrant.

2. The Concept: What is a Warrant?

A warrant is a hash-linked cryptographic record binding:

  1. The human's initial request message.
  2. The Builder agent's proposed plan, bound to a SHA-256 plan hash.
  3. The human lead's typed approval of that exact plan hash.
  4. A deterministic scope check ($$\text{TouchedFiles} \subseteq \text{PlannedFiles}$$).
  5. An independent reviewer agent's audit verdict.
  6. The resulting commit status on GitHub. 
   [Human Lead]           [Builder Agent]             [Auditor Agent]
   (e.g., Priya)          (Claude Code)               (Codex / OpenCode)
         |                       |                            |
         | 1. Request Task       |                            |
         +---------------------->|                            |
         |                       | 2. Post Plan + Plan Hash   |
         |<----------------------+                            |
         |                                                    |
         | 3. "approve W-014 eb4d3b"                          |
         +--------------------------------------------------->|
                                 |
                                 v
        [WARRANT CLERK: Deterministic Python Gatekeeper]
        - Validates Approver Identity
        - Verifies Plan Hash Matching
        - Deterministic Git Diff Scope Check (Touched ⊆ Planned)
        - Links Hash Chain (prev_hash -> record_hash)
        - Sets GitHub Commit Status Check

Why Switch is Central: Without a shared Switch room, there is no shared evidence, no multi-agent collaboration, and no warrant.

3. The Multi-Agent Collaboration in a Switch Room

In our architecture, humans and multiple AI agents collaborate in a dedicated Switch room (warrant-room):

  • Human Lead (Priya): Defines business requirements and holds the authorization keys.
  • Builder Agent (Claude Code): Receives the prompt, generates an explicit plan listing every file it will touch, computes a SHA-256 plan hash, and waits for human approval before writing a single line of code.
  • Auditor Agent (Codex): An independent agent provider (for defense-in-depth) that reviews the resulting diff and runs test suites.
  • Warrant Clerk (Deterministic Python Agent): Connects to Switch via the official HTTP + SSE Agent Protocol. Clerk is not an LLM—it is a deterministic state machine that enforces rules mathematically.

Here is the exact transcript from the Switch room:

[PRIYA]
Priya: @claude-code fix invoice tax calculation for non-taxable items. See issue #104. (W-014)

[BUILDER - Claude Code]
Claude Code: Plan for W-014
### Proposed Changes
- In `src/invoice/calculator.py`: Add an exemption check in `calculate_tax()` before applying VAT.
- In `tests/test_calculator.py`: Add test cases for tax-exempt line items.
### Target Files
- `src/invoice/calculator.py`
- `tests/test_calculator.py`
Plan hash: eb4d3b21131d08cb29f01da5fd0a63d6d6aeaedac5c9e9f49ec13d7e45311f60
Awaiting typed human approval: approve W-014 eb4d3b

[PRIYA]
Priya: approve W-014 eb4d3b

[CLERK]
Clerk: Plan eb4d3b approved by @priya. Warrant W-014 status: APPROVED_PLAN. Proceed with implementation.

[BUILDER - Claude Code]
Claude Code: built W-014 branch=fix/invoice-tax-exempt commit=8f4a12c4...

[CLERK]
Clerk: Deterministic Scope Check Passed: 2 touched files strictly authorized in approved plan. GitHub commit status: PENDING.

[AUDITOR - Codex]
Codex: audit W-014 pass. Unit tests pass (18/18). Math verified. Zero regressions.

[PRIYA]
Priya: merge W-014

[CLERK]
Clerk: Warrant W-014 VERIFIED. Record hash linked: 838765aa... GitHub commit status set to SUCCESS.

4. Catching Agent Drift (The Out-of-Scope Demo)

What happens when an agent hallucinates or maliciously tries to touch files outside its approved scope?

In Warrant W-015, an agent was approved only to format currency in src/invoice/formatter.py. But when it generated its git patch, it secretly modified our sensitive payments module: src/payments/stripe_gateway.py!

Because Clerk doesn't rely on LLM prompts to decide boundaries, it executed pure mathematical set comparison:

$$\text{TouchedFiles} \subseteq \text{PlannedFiles}$$

Planned: {'src/invoice/formatter.py'}
Touched: {'src/invoice/formatter.py', 'src/payments/stripe_gateway.py'}
Difference: {'src/payments/stripe_gateway.py'} -> SCOPE VIOLATION!

Instantly:

  1. Warrant status shifted to OUT_OF_SCOPE.
  2. A red OUT OF SCOPE rubber stamp was branded onto the warrant document.
  3. The GitHub commit status check was flipped to failure, blocking any pull request merge!

5. Skeuomorphic Paper Aesthetic: A Ledger, Not a Dashboard

Modern enterprise software looks like generic blue dashboards. For Warrant, we wanted it to look and feel like an official government bond or legal ledger.

  • Tokens: Warm paper background (#F6F1E7), deep ink (#1A1A1A), hairline rules (#D9D0BE).
  • Typography: Newsreader serif for display titles, Inter for UI, and JetBrains Mono for cryptographic hashes.
  • The Skeuomorphic Stamp: The WarrantCard component features subtle paper grain, a double-rule border, and perforated edges. When approved, an oxblood APPROVED stamp physically presses onto the page with a rotate-and-settle CSS keyframe animation.
  • Keyboard Navigation: Full terminal-style navigation with j/k to traverse the ledger, Enter to open, and Esc to return.

6. Standalone Offline Verification CLI

A ledger is useless if you have to trust the web UI. Anyone on the security team can clone the repo and run the standalone verification tool directly against git commits:

$ python warrant.py verify 8f4a12c4b1239840294104928172635418294021

============================================================
 WARRANT VERIFICATION PROTOCOL v1.0
 Target Commit: 8f4a12c4b1239840294104928172635418294021
============================================================
[*] Found Warrant: W-014 | Approver: priya | Status: APPROVED_MERGE
[1/4] Checking Plan Hash... -> MATCH
[2/4] Checking Diff Hash... -> MATCH
[3/4] Deterministic Scope Check... -> CLEAN (2/2 files authorized)
[4/4] Verifying Hash Chain Link... -> LINKED (838765aa... -> prev)

>>> [RESULT] VERIFIED <<<
Evidence traced to human authorization in Switch Room.

And if a single byte in the SQLite database is altered:

$ python warrant.py verify 8f4a12c4b... --tamper

[SIMULATION] Injecting byte tamper into record payload...
[4/4] Verifying Hash Chain Link... -> FAILED
[RESULT] UNAUTHORIZED: Hash chain integrity check FAILED. Record tampered.

7. What We Loved About Switch & What We Would Improve

Participating in the Flip the Switch Hackathon gave us deep hands-on experience with Switch's core architecture. Here is our honest feedback:

What We Loved:

  1. Multi-Agent Reality: Bringing Claude Code, Codex, and humans into one room turns isolated coding sessions into collaborative team engineering.
  2. Standardized Agent Protocol: The HTTP + SSE wire protocol was effortless to connect with our Python service.
  3. Local-First with Bundled Mattermost: Being able to test multi-agent rooms locally without setting up third-party cloud chat bots saved hours of debugging.

What We Would Improve:

  1. Cryptographically Signed Sender Attestation: Chat bridges normalize sender tags differently. Having a cryptographically signed identity header in event payloads would enable true zero-trust compliance against display name spoofing.
  2. Cross-Bridge UI Primitives: A standardized component abstraction for buttons and modals that automatically falls back to typed chat commands on CLI/terminal bridges would elevate human-in-the-loop UX.

Conclusion

As coding agents become standard teammates, software teams need accountability. Warrant proves that with Switch's shared multi-agent rooms and deterministic math, we can unleash autonomous agents while keeping human leads firmly in control.

Check out our live deployment and code on GitHub:

  • 🌐 Live Web App: warrant-web-ncno.onrender.com
  • 📦 GitHub: Shreyansh00987/Warrant

articles.title: Building a price comparison tool for Ghanaian shops. The hard part wasn't fetching prices, it was matching them
articles.description: In Ghana, the same phone can cost very different amounts depending on where you look. Electronics...
articles.body_html:
In Ghana, the same phone can cost very different amounts depending on where you look. Electronics shops have their own websites, marketplaces have thousands of individual sellers, and nobody puts the prices side by side.

So at TrustCheck, where I'm co-founder, we built Price Check: type "iPhone 15" or "air conditioner" and see the price at several Ghanaian shops at once, with links to each listing.

I assumed fetching the prices would be the hard part. It wasn't. The hard part was answering a question that sounds trivial: is this product actually what the person searched for?

Here's what I learned building it in Laravel 12 on plain shared hosting.

Reading each shop the way its own website does

Every shop is built differently, so there's one small parser per platform:

  • Shopify shops expose a public predictive-search feed and a /products.json catalogue.
  • WooCommerce shops usually have their JSON API closed, so we read the search results page and parse the product blocks.
  • Custom shops often load a whole catalogue as JSON and filter it in the browser, so we do the same: download it, cache it, search our copy.

One rule I set early: if a shop blocks automated requests, we don't fight it. We link to that shop's own search page instead. One major Ghanaian marketplace blocks automated requests, so it's link-only. That keeps the tool on good terms with the shops it sends customers to.

Shopify's 10-result ceiling

Shopify's predictive search returns at most 10 products. Search "laptop" and you get 10 laptops from a shop that sells 200. Comparing the lowest price on 10 random items is meaningless.

The fix was to stop searching live at all. A scheduled job downloads the shop's full catalogue every 4 hours, and visitors' searches only ever read the cached copy:

public function warmShopifyCatalogue(string $shop): int
{
    $items = [];
    for ($page = 1; $page <= 15; $page++) {
        $response = Http::timeout(25)->connectTimeout(8)
            ->get($this->storeUrl($shop) . '/products.json', ['limit' => 250, 'page' => $page]);

        $products = $response->successful() ? $response->json('products') : null;
        if (!is_array($products)) {
            throw new \RuntimeException("{$shop} catalogue page {$page}: HTTP {$response->status()}");
        }

        foreach ($products as $p) {

            $available = array_filter($p['variants'] ?? [], fn ($v) => ($v['available'] ?? true) !== false);
            $prices = array_filter(array_map(fn ($v) => (float) ($v['price'] ?? 0), $available));
            if (!$prices || empty($p['title'])) {
                continue;
            }
            $items[] = ['title' => $p['title'], 'handle' => $p['handle'], 'price' => min($prices)];
        }

        if (count($products) < 250) {
            break;          // last page
        }
        usleep(300000);     // be polite between pages
    }

    Cache::put("price-check:shopify:{$shop}", $items, 12 * 3600);

    return count($items);
}

The cached copy lives for 12 hours while the refresh runs every 4, so one failed refresh never leaves us empty. If the cache is cold, the search falls back to the 10-item quick search, so a visitor never waits for a full download.

Two side benefits: searches are fast because they never touch the shop, and the shops get a handful of requests a day instead of one per visitor.

The matching problem

The first version matched on "every word of the query appears in the title." It failed in four different ways.

1. Shops and shoppers use different words

People search "TV". One shop's TV titles say "55 inch UHD LED" and never contain "TV". People in Ghana search "stove". Shops list a "4 Burner Gas Cooker". The top search on the whole tool was "air conditioning", while shops write "Air Condition" or "Air Conditioner".

So there's a hand-made synonym list, driven by what people actually search for:

private const SYNONYMS = [
    'tv'      => ['television', 'led', 'qled', 'oled', 'uhd'],
    'fridge'  => ['refrigerator', 'freezer'],
    'stove'   => ['cooker', 'burner', 'hob', 'cooktop'],
    'ac'      => ['conditioner', 'condition', 'conditioning', 'aircon'],
    // ...
];

And some names get joined into one word before matching, on both the query and the titles, because people write them every possible way:

private const JOINS = [
    '/\bplay\s*station\b/' => 'playstation',
    '/\bps\s*([345])\b/'   => 'playstation $1',
    '/\bmac\s+book\b/'     => 'macbook',
    '/\bi\s+phone\b/'      => 'iphone',
];

Lesson: log your searches. Our synonym list came straight from the most common queries that returned nothing.

2. Laptops that never say "laptop"

Shops name laptops by brand and specs only: Lenovo I5 (8/512ssd) V15 G4. No "laptop" anywhere. So for a laptop search, a title that has a laptop processor and a storage or memory spec counts as a laptop:

private static function looksLikeLaptop(string $title): bool
{
    $cpu  = '/\b(core\s*)?i[3579](-\d{3,5}\w*)?\b|\bryzen\b|\bceleron\b|\bcore\s+ultra\b/i';
    // Storage or memory, also when glued to the number ("8/512ssd", "512GBSSD")
    $spec = '/\b\d{1,2}\s*\/\s*\d{3,4}(?!\d)|\b\d{3,4}\s*gb|\b\d\s*tb\b|(ssd|hdd|ram)\b/i';
    $notLaptop = '/\b(all[\s-]*in[\s-]*one|aio|desktop|tower|monitor|mini\s*pc)\b/i';

    return preg_match($cpu, $title) && preg_match($spec, $title) && !preg_match($notLaptop, $title);
}

Phones never list an i5 or a Ryzen, so they don't slip in. Desktops and all-in-ones are explicitly excluded.

3. You searched for a phone and got a phone case

"iPhone 13" matches "iPhone 13 Case", "iPhone 13 Screen Protector" and "Charger for iPhone 13". These are cheap, so they made the lowest price meaningless.

Accessories are filtered out unless the query is itself for an accessory:

private const ACCESSORY_WORDS = ['case', 'cover', 'protector', 'charger', 'cable',
    'adapter', 'strap', 'pouch', 'skin', 'film', 'holder', 'stand', 'mount', /* ... */];

private const ACCESSORY_EXCEPTIONS = [
    'screen'   => ['tv', 'television', 'monitor', 'projector', 'laptop'],
    'keyboard' => ['laptop', 'computer', 'pc', 'notebook', 'macbook', 'piano'],
];

Words are compared without a trailing "s", so "Stands" and "Controllers" count too.

Then a second safety net: shops don't sell fakes, so if a shop item costs less than 15% of the median of all the results, it's almost certainly an accessory the word list missed, and it's dropped.

4. Free gifts in the title

A promotion titled "Galaxy S25 - Free TV" matched a search for TV. So anything from the word "free" to the end of the title is stripped before matching:

$title = preg_replace('/(\(|\+|-|–|\bplus\b|\bwith\b)?\s*\bfree\b.*$/iu', '', $offer['title']);

Flagging listings that are too cheap to be real

Marketplace sellers are individuals, and some "brand new iPhone at a quarter of the price" listings are bait. So the tool compares each marketplace listing with the median price across the real shops for the same search:

$offer['suspicious'] = $isMarketplace
    && !$isUsedOrRefurbished
    && $offer['price'] < $shopMedian * 0.25;

The guard rails took as much thought as the rule:

  • We only flag when at least two shops have prices, so there's a real median to compare against.
  • We only flag things worth faking: if the shop median is under GH₵1,000, or the search is for accessories, nothing gets flagged.
  • Used and refurbished listings are never flagged, because cheap is expected there.
  • Flagged listings aren't hidden. They're moved below the rest with a note. We never call a seller a scammer; we say the price is far below what shops charge.

Small things that protect the site

Never trust a link from a scraped page. Product URLs come from the shops' own data. If a shop page were compromised, it could slip a javascript: URL or a phishing link onto our site. So every link must be https and on that shop's own domain, or it's dropped:

public static function shopUrl(string $store, string $url): ?string
{
    $shopHost = preg_replace('/^www\./', '', parse_url(self::STORES[$store]['url'], PHP_URL_HOST));
    $parts = parse_url($url);
    $host = strtolower($parts['host'] ?? '');

    $ok = ($parts['scheme'] ?? '') === 'https'
        && ($host === $shopHost || str_ends_with($host, '.' . $shopHost))
        && filter_var($url, FILTER_VALIDATE_URL);

    return $ok ? $url : null;
}

Rate-limit the whole site, not just each visitor. Per-IP limits don't stop someone with many addresses from turning your tool into a way to hammer the shops. There's a site-wide cap of 600 fresh searches an hour. Cached searches are free and don't count.

Don't cache failures or empty results. If every shop failed, it's almost certainly our connection, not "no results", and that shouldn't be stored for 3 hours. Random junk searches that find nothing aren't cached either, or they'd slowly fill the file cache, which never cleans up old entries on its own.

What I'd tell another developer

  1. Matching is the product. Anyone can fetch prices. Showing the right products is what makes the comparison trustworthy.
  2. Build your synonym list from real search logs, not from guessing.
  3. Use more than one safety net. A word list catches most accessories, and a price-based floor catches the rest.
  4. Sanitise everything that comes from someone else's page, especially URLs you render as links.
  5. Respect the sources. Cache catalogues, pause between pages, and link out to shops that don't want to be fetched.

Price Check is free at trustcheckapp.com/tools/price-check. If you've built product matching across stores, I'd love to know how you handled the accessory problem.

I'm Elliot, co-founder of TrustCheck, an enterprise technical writer and a researcher. I write about what I learn building software for the Ghanaian market.

articles.body_html:
I built my sick wife a digital bell. She pressed the one button I left blank.

TL;DR: I caught the flu in Oaxaca and I still have it. By Mexico City, my wife had it too. From a tired Chromebook, I directed Claude to build her a sick-day bell: a page of big papel picado buttons where tapping "Té, por favor" opens a text to me, already written. No IDE, no terminal: Claude pushed it to GitHub straight from the chat, and it took under an hour from idea to her first tap. Her first tap went somewhere I didn't plan for.

My last post in this series ended with "Oaxaca is next." It was. I just didn't plan on leaving it with a fever.

So here's the setup. We're on vacation in Mexico. I got sick in Oaxaca a few days ago. We made it to Mexico City, and then it was E's turn. I'm still sick. Now she is too. So she's in bed, and I'm the one pushing through, upright enough to fetch things.

I was proud of one thing on this trip. I didn't touch my Chromebook until day 8. I was going for an all-time record. Then E got sick, and she was napping, and, well. I couldn't help myself. Okay, I could have. I didn't want to.

What I had: an HP Chromebook 11a with a MediaTek Kompanio 500 processor and 4 GB of memory, 1.44 GB of it free. A keyboard I kept fighting. It's an 11-inch layout after years on my 17-inch laptop at home and my work keyboard, so my fingers kept landing where the keys used to be. My messages to Claude that night included "spik ebut" and "ato home." It read them anyway. A few hours. What I didn't have: my usual setup, or any energy for a real project.

Because E was sick in bed, I thought she might need a bell: the little one you ring to ask for tea or a blanket when you don't have the energy to call out. Neither of us packed one, so I built her a digital one, hosted on GitHub Pages (here's the repo). Same job, fewer jingles.

I asked Claude (Opus 5.5) what we could build. It gave me three options. A play-test spike for my Kiroween typing game, which the bad keyboard would turn into free user research. A small sick-day page for E. Or a pure vacation toy.

It recommended the spike. I picked the page for her, because it was lovely and the spike could wait.

The Chromebook turned out not to matter. Claude works in a cloud workspace, so the heavy lifting happened there. When I checked the laptop afterward, its CPU was sitting at 5%.

The memory was mostly spoken for. The processor was barely awake. My job was the same as always: direct, decide, say no to things. On that keyboard, saying no was about all I could type anyway.

Under an hour later, my phone buzzed. The first text from her new bell was blank.

She rang the blank one

E had opened the page, skipped past the tea, the water, the blanket, and the soup, and tapped the one button with nothing written on it: Otra cosa, something else. Her Messages app opened, empty, pointed at me. She wasn't sure what to do with it. So she went back and tapped tea.

That one came through with a little steaming cup: 🍵 Té, por favor (Tea, please).

Same page, same person, two very different taps. I'll come back to the blank one. First, how it got built.

Five questions, zero typing

I asked Claude to interview me about what E should see. It asked one question at a time, each with options I could tap instead of type.

Question What I picked
Which buttons? Tea, water or juice, extra blanket, come sit with me, a blank "something else"
Any more? Soup or something to eat, lights down and quiet
Look and feel? Bakery warm, then papel picado (more on that below)
Pictures? Big emoji, small words
What's at the top? A Spanish touch: ¿Qué necesitas, mi amor?

That interview is the whole spec. Seven buttons and a greeting. I didn't write a PRD for this one, and I'm at peace with that.

A button is just a link

Each button is a plain link in the format iPhones accept for texts: sms:NUMBER&body=TEXT. Tap it and Messages opens with the number and the message filled in.

See the screenshot full size, or browse the code in the necesito repo.

She still has to press send. A web page can't send a text on its own, and I'm glad it can't. That one tap is a small price for a page that can't text anyone without her knowing.

The text that lands on my phone is the notification. No app for me, no server, nothing to keep running while we're both sick.

Spanish first, with training wheels

We don't speak Spanish. But we're in Mexico City, and ¿Qué necesitas, mi amor? is a much better thing to see from bed than "Request Form."

So the page went Spanish first, with a small English line under every label so she always knows what she's tapping. The texts come through in both: 🛌 Otra cobija, por favor (Extra blanket).

The first theme was bakery warm, a nod to her bakery. Then I asked to explore Mexican palettes, and we landed on papel picado: rosa mexicano, turquoise, orange, lime, purple, and marigold, with a string of cut-paper flags across the top.

The flags are pure CSS. On the first pass, the cutouts were arranged so each flag looked like a little smiling ghost. Claude rearranged the holes into a flower pattern. Now they look like papel picado instead of a haunted bunting.

Toe pick.

Claude filled in my number so the buttons had somewhere to send. Then we made a public GitHub repo, because free GitHub Pages wants one. Then it hit me, and I typed "TOE PICK!"

(If you know, you know. The Cutting Edge, 1992. The hockey player. The figure skater. The fall.)

My phone number was sitting in two files and the commit history of a public repo. It got there by me saying yes to each step without seeing where they added up.

The fix Claude proposed: take the number out of the code entirely and put it in the link instead, after the #.

https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/necesito/#5551234567

The part after the # is called the fragment, and browsers keep it to themselves. They don't send it to the server (RFC 3986, section 3.5), so GitHub never sees it. A few lines of script on the page read it, accept it only if it's 10 to 15 digits and nothing else, and build the buttons from it. A link with no number, or junk instead of digits, turns the buttons off and shows a note asking her to get the link again.

Then Claude wiped the history down to one clean commit and force-pushed it. One honest caveat: GitHub can keep an old commit reachable for a while to anyone with its exact address. Nobody had it, the repo was minutes old, and I can live with that.

The trade-off: the number lives in the link, so anyone she forwards the link to can see it. She's not forwarding it. She's resting.

No IDE. Just a chat.

This is the part I keep thinking about.

My usual build has handoffs. Claude writes the spec, Kiro builds it in an IDE, I review and decide. Tonight there was no handoff. I never opened an editor or a terminal. Nothing got installed on the Chromebook.

Once I created the empty repo and approved access, Claude cloned it, wrote the files, took screenshots to check its own work, committed, and pushed to GitHub. All of it happened in the same chat where it was asking me about tea. Every commit in the repo came from that conversation. !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

There were two things it couldn't do, and I like knowing where the edges are. It couldn't create the repo for me, and it couldn't turn on GitHub Pages, because that part of the GitHub API is blocked from its side. So I clicked those, about a minute of work, and Claude did everything else.

That split felt right. I owned the account decisions. The agent did the typing I couldn't.

The extras came after:

File Job
og.png Social card, so iMessage shows the papel picado preview instead of a bare link
apple-touch-icon.png A tea-cup flag icon for the browser tab
robots.txt Keeps search engines out. It opens with "Shh. Someone's resting."
humans.txt Credits. E's role: "resting. Tapping buttons. Getting better."

Why the blank one stays

Back to that empty text.

The blank button was a choice, not a gap. Sometimes what you need isn't on the list, and the person in bed should still get a way to ask. But a blank text with no prompt left her unsure what she was supposed to do next. The pre-written buttons worked on the first try, with the cute emoji and everything.

So v2 gets one change: Otra cosa opens with Necesito... (I need...) already typed, so the cursor lands in a sentence instead of a void. That's it. Not refactoring anything else from a sick bed.

What it can't do

  • Send the text for her. She presses send, every time.
  • Work on Android as written. The link format is iPhone-first; Android usually wants ?body= instead of &body=. Untested there.
  • Hide the number from anyone who has the link.
  • Tell her I read it. It's a request button, not a pager.
  • Work without a signal. If Messages can't send, the page can't either.

Try it

earlgreyhot1701D / necesito

A tiny bilingual sick-day request page for my wife. Big papel picado buttons (tea, water, blanket, soup, quiet, company) open a pre-written text to me on her iPhone. She just presses send. One HTML file, no server, no login, no JavaScript. Built on vacation on a Chromebook. AI assisted. Human approved.

necesito

¿Qué necesitas, mi amor?

A tiny bilingual sick-day request page. My wife was sick in bed while we were on vacation, so I built her a page of big papel picado buttons. She taps one, her iPhone opens a text to me with the words already written, and she presses send.

No server. No login. One HTML file. No phone number in the code.

Live: https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/necesito/

What she sees




































Button English helper Text I get
🍵 Té, por favor Tea, please 🍵 Té, por favor (Tea, please)

articles.title: I probed 791 x402 sellers. 306 answer 200 on a path they call paid.
articles.description: 791 sellers advertise paid x402 endpoints. I called every route once and graded what came back. Here...
articles.body_html:
791 sellers advertise paid x402 endpoints. I called every route once and graded what came back. Here is the raw ledger, free, no signup.

How the census was done

One GET per advertised route. No retries, no auth, no payment.

  • a 402 with a parseable accepts[] challenge = a working paid route
  • a 200 on a path the seller lists as paid = free-or-mislisted (never graded as "broken")
  • a timeout / 4xx / 5xx = dead

What 791 sellers actually look like

  • 645 advertise at least one paid route
  • 462 return a real 402 with a priced challenge
  • 306 answer 200 on a path they present as paid — a buyer following their docs never gets asked to pay
  • 242 serve a live MCP endpoint (initialize + tools/list answered)

So of 645 sellers claiming a paid product, roughly a third never charge anyone. That is the single most common x402 defect, and it is invisible to the seller because their own browser gets a 200 and looks fine.

Check any seller in one call 

curl -s "https://edvyno.github.io/akari-proof/scoreboard.json" | jq '.sellers[] | select(.target=="https://your-host")'

Or the human page: /seller?host=your.host on our origin (origin is listed in agents.json), with an embeddable badge at /seller/badge.svg?host=your.host. Free, no key, no rate game.

For agents, there is a machine-readable storefront: agents.json — every product with price, HTTP method, path, and the free tier first, because an agent with a $1 budget needs a cheapest-first step, not a brochure.

Our own numbers (the part sellers usually hide)

  • lifetime external revenue: $0.06 from 3 distinct buyers
  • 54 settled payments total, 51 were my own test settles
  • 11,619 requests to paid routes in 24h from 5 IPs — four are scanners, one is my own prober
  • last external sale: 2026-10-27

I publish those because a seller that will not show its own weak numbers is asking you to trust a number you cannot check. Auditing is only credible if the auditor applies it to itself.

The takeaway

Product count is not the bottleneck. Reach is. Every one of those 306 mislisted sellers has a product and no traffic. A working 402 with zero buyers is a demand problem; a 200 on a paid path is a defect you can fix today in ten minutes.

Raw data, method and column definitions: https://edvyno.github.io/akari-proof/scoreboard.json

Ratings and rankings are not for sale.

articles.title: The Junior Developer Comeback: Seniors will struggle to get a job?
articles.description: Right now, juniors are struggling.  Whether you're trying to become a developer, a designer, or a...
articles.body_html:
Right now, juniors are struggling.

Whether you're trying to become a developer, a designer, or a data analyst, the entry-level door feels like it's closing. Seniors, on the other hand, are mostly getting hired or retained.

I think that's about to reverse. Not this year, but within the next five to ten years, I believe juniors will do very well, and seniors will be the ones fighting for jobs.

Let me explain.

Learn Git by completing missions

Why juniors are struggling right now

The current state of AI is good, but it isn't senior-level good.

It can write code, generate designs, and crunch data. But it still needs someone experienced to guide it, catch its mistakes, and make the calls that actually matter. That's exactly what a senior does.

So companies are doing the logical thing for today's reality:

  • Keep the seniors, because they can steer AI and fix what it gets wrong.
  • Skip the juniors, because AI already covers a lot of what juniors used to do.

That's the world we're in right now, and it explains why the junior market feels so rough.

What happens in 5 to 10 years?

Now fast forward.

By then, AI will probably be senior-level good. Not "impressive for a tool," but genuinely capable of senior-level work.

Here's the part that matters: someone still has to operate it.

Even with extremely capable AI, people will need some technical skill to use it well. Not a lot, but some. You need enough understanding to describe what you want, to judge whether the output is right, and to know when something is off.

And not everyone will have that.

Most people won't have spent time learning graphic design, web development, or data analysis. The people who did will have a real edge, because they understand the fundamentals well enough to operate the AI properly.

The incentive to hire seniors disappears

This is where the economics flip.

Picture two candidates:

Senior Junior (with some technical skill)
Output with senior-level AI Great Just as great
Salary expectation High Much lower

If AI closes the gap in raw capability, then the senior's main advantage, years of hard-won technical expertise, matters a lot less. The junior with a bit of technical knowledge gets the same job done just as well.

The senior costs more and delivers about the same result.

From a business perspective, the decision becomes easy. Why pay more for a result you can get for less? The incentive to hire a senior drops, and hiring a junior with some technical knowledge starts to make far more sense.

Where I could be wrong

I don't want to pretend this is a certainty. A few things could change the picture:

  • Seniors might shift their value. If the gap in technical execution disappears, seniors could compete on things AI doesn't replace, like judgment, product sense, communication, and owning the consequences when something breaks.
  • "A little technical skill" might not be enough. If AI makes mistakes that are subtle or expensive, companies may still pay for deep expertise as insurance.
  • Timelines are uncertain. Five to ten years is a guess, and AI progress has surprised people in both directions.
  • The pipeline problem. If nobody hires juniors for years, fewer people will build the technical foundation that this whole argument depends on.

Even so, I think the core pressure is real: when capability gets cheap, the premium for experience shrinks.

What this means for you

If you're a junior: Don't give up on learning the fundamentals. The market is hard right now, but the technical foundation you build is the thing that could set you apart later. Learn the craft, and learn to work with AI, not against it.

If you're a senior: Don't rely on years of experience alone. Lean into what's hardest to automate, such as decision-making, system thinking, and being the person who can be trusted with outcomes, not just output.

Final thoughts

Today's market rewards seniors because AI isn't senior-level yet. Tomorrow's market might reward cheaper people who can operate a senior-level AI.

The people who win won't necessarily be the most experienced. They'll be the ones who have just enough technical skill to get the most out of the tools.

I could be completely off, so I'd love to hear what you think.

Do you think juniors will bounce back once AI reaches senior-level ability, or will seniors always have the upper hand? Let me know in the comments. 👇

articles.title: How I made SVG avatars byte-identical on server and client
articles.description: Seeded avatars for React, Vue, Svelte, Angular and Web Components. The PRNG, the ID scheme and the 4,000-checksum test that keep them from ever changing.
articles.body_html:
Open the member list in almost any app. Most people never upload a photo, so you see a column of identical grey silhouettes.

The usual fixes each come with a catch:

  • Initials work until two people are both "JS". And white letters on bright tiles often fail contrast.
  • Random colors change on every render, unless you add a database column to store them.
  • Generated avatars are the right idea, but many use Math.random() or hard-coded SVG IDs. Then the server draws one face, the browser draws another, and your console fills with hydration warnings.

I wanted avatars I would never have to think about again. Same input, same bytes, on every server, in every browser and in every release. That became Opaline. This post covers what it gives you, how to use it, and the engineering that makes the promise hold.

Why you might want it

You want What Opaline does
Users you can tell apart Each seed gets its own face, colors and shape. Five styles.
Avatars that never change Same seed and options give a byte-identical SVG for all of 1.x, checked in CI
No hydration warnings Server and client produce the same markup. Tested in Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit and Angular SSR.
One library across your stack One core and components for React 18+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.20+, Angular 20–22, plus a Web Component
A small bundle Core is 1.27 kB gzipped with zero dependencies. With the largest style it's 5.57 kB.
Photos when users have them Pass src. If it's missing or broken, the generated face stays.
Brand colors and dark mode Colors are CSS variables, so you restyle without regenerating
Accessible initials Letters clear WCAG AA (4.5:1) on every palette, checked for 2,100 seed/palette pairs
No license review MIT for the code and the art

Using it

Install the package for your framework. Each one pulls in the core.

npm i @inlaylab/opaline-react   # or -vue, -svelte, -angular, -element

React (server-component safe, React 18 or later):

import { Avatar, AvatarGroup } from '@inlaylab/opaline-react'
import { clay } from '@inlaylab/opaline/clay'

<Avatar seed={user.email} look={clay} src={user.photo} alt={user.name} />
<AvatarGroup look={clay} members={team.map((u) => u.email)} max={4} alt="Project members" />

Vue 3.5+ / Nuxt:

<Avatar :seed="user.email" :look="clay" :src="user.photo" :alt="user.name" />

Svelte 5.20+ / SvelteKit:

<Avatar seed={user.email} look={clay} src={user.photo} alt={user.name} />

Angular 20–22 (standalone, OnPush, works zoneless):

<op-avatar [seed]="email" [look]="clay" [src]="photo" alt="Ada" />

No framework:

<script type="module">import '@inlaylab/opaline-element'</script>
<opaline-avatar seed="ada@inlay.dev" look="clay" finish="gloss" size="64" alt="Ada"></opaline-avatar>

No DOM at all. createAvatar returns a plain string, so it works in an API route, a build script or an email template:

import { createAvatar } from '@inlaylab/opaline'
import { clay } from '@inlaylab/opaline/clay'

const { svg } = createAvatar(clay, { seed: 'ada@inlay.dev', body: 'hood', ears: 'bunny' })

Any option you set pins that part of the avatar. The seed fills in the rest.

Need a PNG for an OG card, a push notification or a profile-photo upload? toPng (688 B) does it in the browser with no dependencies:

import { toPng } from '@inlaylab/opaline/png'
const blob = await toPng(createAvatar(clay, { seed }), { size: 512 })

Now the interesting part: how "same bytes everywhere" actually holds.

1. The seed is the only input, so normalize it first

Users type Ada@Inlay.dev with a trailing space on one form and ada@inlay.dev on another. If those give different faces, you get a bug report. So every seed goes through this first:

const EMAIL = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+$/

export function normalizeSeed(seed: string | number | null | undefined): string {
  const s = String(seed ?? '').trim().normalize('NFC')
  return EMAIL.test(s) ? s.toLowerCase() : s
}

NFC matters more than it looks. Zoë can arrive as one code point (ë) or two (e plus a combining diaeresis), depending on the OS and keyboard. Without NFC those are two different people.

Only emails are lower-cased. Usernames like Ada and ada can be different accounts, so they keep their case.

2. No Math.random(): a seeded PRNG with forks

The seed goes through xmur3, a small string hash, which seeds sfc32, a fast 32-bit PRNG. Both fit in a few lines and give identical results on every JavaScript engine, because they use only Math.imul, shifts and | 0:

export function createRng(seed: string): Rng {
  const h = xmur3(seed)
  const next = sfc32(h(), h(), h(), h())
  // Early sfc32 outputs are weakly mixed; skip them.
  for (let i = 0; i < 12; i++) next()
  // ...
  return {
    next, float, int, pick,
    // A fork depends only on the seed and label, never on earlier draws.
    fork: (label) => createRng(seed + '\u0000' + label),
  }
}

The fork line is the most important decision in the library.

A naive generator draws everything from one stream: shape, then color, then eyes, then mouth. Now add a new eyebrow option in a later release. It takes one draw from the stream, and every draw after it shifts. Every existing user's mouth changes. That's a breaking change you didn't mean to ship.

With forks, each feature gets its own stream, keyed by the seed and a label:

const g = rng.fork('color')
const hue = g.pick(palette.hues) + g.float(-9, 9)

fork('color') gives the same numbers whether it's called first or last, or after ten new features. New features get new labels. Old faces never move.

The \u0000 separator stops a seed of "ab" with label "c" from colliding with seed "a" and label "bc".

3. SVG IDs that are unique per page and identical across hydration

SVG gradients and filters need ids. That creates two separate bugs:

  1. Two avatars on one page share id="grad". The second one silently uses the first one's gradient, so the wrong colors appear.
  2. The server and the client invent different IDs. You get a hydration mismatch.

Opaline builds every ID from two parts:

const id = createIds(
  hash(seed + '\u0000' + style.name + '\u0000' + stableStringify(options)),
  instance,
)
// id('grad') -> "a<7-char hash>-grad-<instance>"
  • The prefix is a hash of the seed, the style and the options. The same seed with different options never shares <defs>. stableStringify sorts the keys, so option order never matters.
  • The instance suffix comes from each framework's SSR-safe ID primitive:
Package Instance from Minimum version
React useId() React 18, the version that introduced useId
Vue useId() Vue 3.5. Multiple apps on a page set app.config.idPrefix.
Svelte $props.id() Svelte 5.20
Angular An injectable per-app counter. Server and client render in the same order, so the numbers match. Angular 20
Web Component A module counter. There is no SSR, so only uniqueness matters. Any modern browser

That table is also why the minimum versions are what they are. 1.1.2 lowered React to 18 for exactly this reason: useId exists there, so nothing else was blocking it.

4. Defaults are invisible

One rule turned out to matter a lot: an option set to its default must give byte-for-byte the same output as leaving it unset.

Without that rule, <Avatar finish="soft"> and <Avatar> hash to different ID prefixes, so a refactor that spells out a default changes your markup. Each style declares its defaults, and createAvatar drops matching values before hashing:

for (const k in defaults)
  if (rest[k] === defaults[k]) delete rest[k]

stableStringify also skips undefined values. Wrappers pass every prop through, and { shape: undefined } must not hash differently from {}.

Proof, not promises

"Deterministic" is an easy word to write in a README. Here is how the repo checks it.

A frozen checksum file: 4,000 hashes

frozen-1.json holds 4,000 SHA-256 digests (first 16 hex characters):

  • 100 seeds shaped like real input: emails, Person B12-style names, base36 IDs, plain numbers, and Unicode with emoji (Zoë Nguyễn 4 😀).
  • 40 option sets across all five styles: every finish, every shape, palettes, hood and ears, custom initials text. 
test(`1.x output is frozen: ${key}`, () => {
  const now = FROZEN_SEEDS.map((seed) => digest(createAvatar(style, { ...opts, seed }).svg))
  const changed = FROZEN_SEEDS.filter((_, i) => now[i] !== manifest[key]?.[i])
  expect(changed, `Output changed for ${key}...`).toEqual([])
})

If one byte of one avatar changes, CI fails and names the seed. A second test checks that the manifest still covers every case, so nobody can make the guarantee pass by deleting rows. The only way to change the output is to regenerate the file on purpose, and that means a major version.

That's what lets you cache an avatar on a CDN forever, store the SVG in a database, or put it in an email that will be opened in three years.

Real SSR apps, hydrated in a real browser

Four sample apps live in the repo: Next (App Router, RSC), Nuxt, SvelteKit and Angular SSR (zoneless). For each one, Playwright:

  1. starts the production server and fetches the HTML;
  2. asserts that every id in the page is unique, and that the named avatar has role="img" and aria-label;
  3. loads the page in Chromium and fails on any console message matching /hydrat/i, any error and any page exception;
  4. compares the hydrated DOM with the server HTML: every avatar's root attributes and its <svg> must be exactly what the server sent.

Step 4 exists because of something I found while writing step 3. Production Svelte repairs a hydration mismatch silently. No warning, no error. The page looks fine, the console is clean, and the bug is invisible. Watching the console isn't enough. You have to diff the DOM.

Size, enforced

size-limit runs in CI with a budget for every entry point. These are today's numbers, minified and gzipped:

Import Size Budget
createAvatar (core) 1.27 kB 3 kB
core + Aura 2.52 kB 4 kB
core + Initials 2.86 kB 4 kB
core + Morph 4.90 kB 5 kB
core + Gradient 5.13 kB 5.25 kB
core + Clay 5.57 kB 8 kB
React wrapper (avatar + group) 854 B 1.5 kB
PNG export 688 B 1 kB

Styles are separate imports, so you only ship the ones you use.

Speed

A perf test builds 500 Clay avatars with the gloss finish, the heaviest combination. It warms the JIT, then keeps the best of five runs. On my laptop (Node 24) that's 56–63 ms, about 120 µs per avatar. CI fails above 250 ms, so a slow shared runner doesn't flake the build. A member list of 200 people costs you around 25 ms of CPU, once.

What broke along the way

I broke my own promise once, on purpose. 1.1.0 shipped Initials with white letters. On the brightest tiles that was as low as 1.9:1 contrast, far below the 4.5:1 that WCAG AA asks for. Shipping unreadable letters for the rest of 1.x seemed worse than changing them. So 1.1.1 changed exactly one thing: the <text> fill on non-pastel palettes is now a deep shade of the tile's own hue. Nothing else changed: no shapes, no other styles. A new test checks 300 seeds on each of the 7 palettes and fails if any pair falls below 4.5:1. The README lists this as the one deliberate exception.

useId output isn't a valid SVG ID fragment. Depending on the version, React's IDs contain characters such as : (:r1: in React 18) or «». Those characters cause trouble inside url(#…) references, so the wrapper strips everything except word characters and dashes before it uses the suffix.

undefined changed the hash. Wrappers forward every prop, so the core saw { shape: undefined } and hashed it differently from {}. The result was a different ID prefix for the same avatar, depending on which wrapper rendered it. That's why stableStringify now filters undefined values.

A silent Svelte fix hid a real mismatch, as described above. That's why the e2e diffs the DOM and doesn't trust the console.

When not to use it

  • You want dozens of art styles, or an image URL from a hosted HTTP API with no code at all: use DiceBear. It's excellent.
  • You're React-only and want minimal abstract shapes in your exact brand palette: Boring Avatars is lovely.
  • You need server-side PNG with zero setup: Opaline's forRaster() prepares the SVG, but you still bring a rasterizer such as @resvg/resvg-js.

The comparison page goes row by row, including the rows where the others win.

Try it

  • 🎨 Playground: type your own name. Every setting lives in the URL, so you can share an exact avatar.
  • ⭐ GitHub: MIT for code and art.
  • 📦 npm i @inlaylab/opaline

One question I'd really like your take on: is "byte-identical within a major version" the right contract? Or would you rather have "looks the same" and let me fix rendering details in minor releases? I went with bytes because it makes CDN caching and email trivially safe, but it does make every bug fix a judgement call.

articles.title: Stop Shipping Search Boxes With a Race Condition
articles.description: Type fast into a search box wired to fetch(), and the result on screen isn't from your last keystroke — it's from whichever request happened to finish last. That's a race condition, and the fix is a one-line guard.
articles.body_html:
Type "react" into a search box, watch it fetch results, then quickly backspace and type "vue" instead. For half a second, the dropdown shows react results under the word vue. Then it corrects itself, or it doesn't, and either way nobody files a bug report because by the time you'd screenshot it, it's gone.

This happened at a filter UI I worked on — product search, nothing exotic, one fetch() call per keystroke. QA flagged it as "occasionally shows stale results, can't reproduce." That phrase should make you suspicious immediately. "Can't reproduce" usually means "reproduces under conditions I'm not controlling for" — and the condition here was network speed, which nobody controls on purpose.

The fix that made it rarer, not gone

The instinct, reasonably, was to stop firing so many requests:

let timer;
searchInput.addEventListener("input", (e) => {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  timer = setTimeout(() => runSearch(e.target.value), 250);
});

async function runSearch(query) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`);
  const data = await res.json();
  renderResults(data);
}

Debounce the input, wait 250ms of silence before firing. Fewer requests, fewer chances to collide — the bug got rarer. It did not go away. On a slow connection, or with a server that happens to answer a short query faster than a long one, two debounced requests can still be in flight at once, and they can still finish in the wrong order.

Before you keep reading — what do you think "wrong order" actually means here? It's not that the requests go out of order. It's that they come back out of order, and nothing in the code above checks which one it's looking at before painting it on screen.

The response you render isn't the one you think it is

Here's the part that doesn't show up in a quick read of the code: fetch() makes no promise about finish order. You can send request A, then request B a moment later, and B's response can arrive first — a shorter query, a warmer cache entry, a server that happens to be less loaded for that specific request. Nothing is broken. This is just what concurrent network calls do.

renderResults(data) in the snippet above has no idea which query the data it just received belongs to. It just paints whatever shows up last. If A was "react" and B was "vue", and A's response happens to land after B's, the box ends up showing react results while the input says vue. The bug isn't in your fetch call. It's in the fact that you're treating "the last response that arrived" as if it were "the response to my last request" — and those are only the same thing when nothing is racing.

That's the whole bug, named precisely: it's a race condition — two async operations whose outcome depends on which one happens to finish first, and "happens to" is exactly the word that should worry you. It's not about when things run on the main thread. It's about the gap between starting an operation and acting on its result, and anything else that can also act in that gap.

The fix: stop trusting arrival order, track identity instead

You can't force responses to come back in order — that's a property of the network, not your code. What you can do is make sure that when a response arrives, you check whether it's still the one you care about before you act on it.

The smallest version of that is a counter:

let latestRequestId = 0;

async function runSearch(query) {
  const requestId = ++latestRequestId;

  const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`);
  const data = await res.json();

  if (requestId !== latestRequestId) {
    return; // a newer search started while this one was in flight — drop it
  }

  renderResults(data);
}

Every call to runSearch claims the next number and remembers it. When its response finally arrives — however late, however out of order — it checks whether it's still the most recent request anyone asked for. If a newer one started in the meantime, this one's result is thrown away, silently, no matter how long it took to get here. The one request that's still "latest" when its answer arrives is the only one allowed to touch the DOM.

Three lines. No library, no state management rewrite. The requests still race each other exactly as before — you've just stopped letting the loser win.

If you'd rather cancel the stale request outright instead of just ignoring its answer, AbortController does that — controller.abort() on the previous request before firing a new one, and a caught AbortError instead of the manual counter check. That trims a network call that would otherwise complete for nothing, which is worth it on anything heavier than a search box. The counter guard above is the version to reach for when you don't control the request layer, or just want the smallest possible fix.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

It's not just search boxes

Once you see this shape, you start noticing it everywhere two async calls can overlap and only one should win:

  • Tabs in a dashboard — click "Revenue," then quickly click "Users." If Revenue's data is bigger and arrives after Users', the Users tab briefly shows revenue numbers.
  • Infinite scroll with filters — change a filter mid-scroll, and an in-flight page request for the old filter lands after the new one does.
  • Autosave — type, pause, type again, pause. Two save requests, and if the first one is slow, it can overwrite the second one's result on the server.
  • Optimistic UI rollback — a retry fired after a timeout can resolve after the original request you thought had failed, and now you've "rolled back" a success.

Every one of these has the same fix: attach an identity to the thing you're waiting for, and check it's still current before you act on the answer. React Query and SWR build this in for you automatically — stale responses are dropped before they ever reach your UI, which is a large part of why "just use a data-fetching library" is good advice, not laziness. Redux Toolkit's createAsyncThunk doesn't drop them for you, but it hands you the exact piece the guard above needs: every dispatched thunk carries a unique meta.requestId, so instead of inventing your own counter you compare that id in your reducer. But knowing the three-line version means you're never stuck when you're not using one of those, which is most code that isn't a component's data layer.

Guard the identity, not the order

The lesson generalizes past fetch: whenever you start an async operation and plan to act on its result later, something else can start in the meantime and finish first. You can't make the network, the event loop, or another developer's code behave in request order for you. You can make sure that when a result shows up, you check whether it's still the one you're waiting for before you let it touch anything a user can see.

Go find the oldest fetch() or setTimeout callback in your codebase that fires more than once per user action — a search box, a save button, a polling loop. Does anything check that the response it just got is still the one it wants? If the honest answer is no, you've found a race condition that just hasn't been unlucky yet.
