articles.title: Your PHP API Sends Keys 10 Then 2. Your TypeScript Client Reads 2 Then 10
articles.description: PHP arrays keep insertion order. JavaScript objects list integer-like keys first, ascending. Why it happens, the array_filter twin, and the fixes.
articles.body_html:
• Book: PHP to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your PHP controller builds the shipping options for a checkout dropdown. Product wants Express on top, so you build the array in that order: ['10' => 'Express', '2' => 'Standard', 'pickup' => 'Store pickup']. The JSON leaves the server with the keys in that order. The TypeScript frontend loops over it with Object.entries, and Standard renders first.

Nobody sorted anything. Both runtimes did exactly what their specs say. A PHP array remembers insertion order for every key. A JavaScript object lists integer-like keys first, in ascending numeric order, and only then the other string keys in the order they were created.

Two languages, two meanings of "in order"

The PHP manual says it in one line: "An array in PHP is actually an ordered map." Int keys and string keys share one sequence, and that sequence is insertion order until you call a sort function.

There is one wrinkle on the way in. The same page explains that strings holding valid decimal integers are cast to int: the key "8" is stored under 8, while "08" stays a string. So '10' and '2' in your literal become int keys 10 and 2. The order survives the cast.

JavaScript objects follow a different rule. The ECMAScript spec algorithm that orders an object's own keys is OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys, and it has three passes:

  1. Every own key that is an array index, "in ascending numeric index order".
  2. Every other string key, "in ascending chronological order of property creation".
  3. Every symbol key, also in creation order.

The APIs you reach for every day sit on top of that. The archived for-in order proposal lists Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries, JSON.parse and JSON.stringify as for-in-ordered APIs, and MDN's for...in page puts the rule plainly: integer keys "will be traversed first in ascending order by value, then other string keys in ascending chronological order of property creation." MDN's Object.keys page shows it with { 100: "a", 2: "b", 7: "c" }, which comes back as ['2', '7', '100'].

Is either side breaking JSON? No. RFC 8259 defines an object as "an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs" and notes that parsers "have been observed to differ as to whether or not they make the ordering of object members visible to calling software." The wire format never promised you order. PHP happened to keep it, and JavaScript applies its own rule.


Same cards, two rules: PHP keeps the line as built, a JavaScript object pulls integer-like keys to the front.

Watch it happen in PHP and Node

Here is the PHP side. Save it as order.php and run php order.php:

<?php
$options = [
    '10' => 'Express',
    '2' => 'Standard',
    'pickup' => 'Store pickup',
];

var_dump(array_keys($options));
// int 10, int 2, string "pickup": insertion order

echo json_encode($options), PHP_EOL;
// a JSON object, keys written as 10, 2, pickup

json_encode writes an object here because, in the manual's words, "if the keys are not a continuous numeric sequence starting from 0, all keys are encoded as strings, and specified explicitly for each key-value pair." Keys 10 and 2 are not a sequence from 0, so you get an object, in PHP's order.

Now the client. Save it as order.mjs and run it with Node.js:

const body =
  '{"10":"Express","2":"Standard","pickup":"Store pickup"}';
const options = JSON.parse(body);

for (const [id, label] of Object.entries(options)) {
  console.log(id, label);
}
// spec order: "2" first, then "10", then "pickup"

The text on the wire still says 10 first. The object built from it lists 2 first, because "2" and "10" are array indices and "pickup" is not. Round-trip it through JSON.stringify and the reordered version is what goes back out: MDN's JSON.stringify page says properties are visited "using the same algorithm as Object.keys()".

TypeScript cannot warn you. JSON.parse returns any, and a Record<string, string> describes both orders identically. Key order is not part of the type system.

Which keys move, exactly

The spec's definition of array index is narrower than "looks like a number". It is a key whose canonical numeric form is an integer from 0 up to 2^32 − 2. That gives you a few edge cases worth knowing:

  • "01" is not in canonical form, so it keeps creation order. PHP agrees here: per the manual, "08" stays a string key too.
  • "-1" and "1.5" are not array indices (one is negative, the other is not an integer), so they keep creation order.
  • "4294967295" (2^32 − 1) and anything larger keeps creation order.

So the reshuffle depends on the values of your keys. A map keyed by small auto-increment IDs gets sorted. The same map keyed by slugs or 64-bit snowflake IDs keeps its order. One endpoint can behave differently in staging and production because the data is different.

The sibling trap: array_filter turns a list into an object

The same rule in json_encode causes a second bug, and this one breaks code instead of reordering it. array_filter does not renumber: "Array keys are preserved, and may result in gaps if the array was indexed." A list with a gap is no longer a continuous sequence from 0, so it goes out as an object.

The manual's own json_encode example shows it: after unset($sequential[1]), the array ["foo","bar","baz","blong"] encodes as {"0":"foo","2":"baz","3":"blong"}.


Remove one item from a PHP list and json_encode stops sending a list.

<?php
$tags = ['php', 'typescript', 'go'];

$kept = array_filter($tags, fn ($t) => $t !== 'php');
echo json_encode($kept), PHP_EOL;
// keys 1 and 2 survive: a JSON object, not an array

echo json_encode(array_values($kept)), PHP_EOL;
// keys reset to 0 and 1: a JSON array

The nasty part is that the shape depends on the data. Filter out 'go' instead and keys 0 and 1 remain, which is still a list, so you get an array. Your TypeScript client calls data.tags.map(...), it works for weeks, and then one request drops the first element and the call throws a TypeError, because a plain object has no map method.

It runs the other way too. The json_encode page shows that an empty array encodes as [], so a PHP map that happens to be empty reaches the client as an array, not {}. JSON_FORCE_OBJECT exists, but it is a blunt switch: the same example turns a nested list [[1,2,3]] into {"0":{"0":1,"1":2,"2":3}}.

Fix it on the PHP side

Treat the JSON shape as part of the API contract and make it explicit.

For lists, call array_values after anything that can leave gaps: array_filter, unset, array_unique. The array_filter manual page points to it for exactly this. On PHP 8.1+, array_is_list checks whether keys are "consecutive numbers from 0 to count($array)-1", which makes a cheap assertion in a response test.

For maps where order matters, stop sending a JSON object. Send a list of records:

<?php
$options = [
    10 => 'Express',
    2 => 'Standard',
    'pickup' => 'Store pickup',
];

$payload = [];
foreach ($options as $id => $label) {
    $payload[] = ['id' => (string) $id, 'label' => $label];
}

echo json_encode($payload), PHP_EOL;
// a JSON array of {id, label} objects, Express first

The (string) cast matters. PHP already turned '10' into int 10, so without it id is a JSON number for numeric keys and a string for 'pickup'. Your TypeScript type would have to be number | string. Cast once on the server and the client gets one type.

Fix it on the TypeScript side

Type the payload as the list it is, and build a Map if you need lookups by ID. MDN states that a Map "remembers the original insertion order of the keys", and that holds for "10" and "2" as much as for "pickup":

type ShippingOption = { id: string; label: string };

async function loadOptions(): Promise<Map<string, string>> {
  const res = await fetch('/api/shipping-options');
  const list = (await res.json()) as ShippingOption[];
  return new Map(list.map((o) => [o.id, o.label]));
}

The same MDN page is blunt about plain objects: their order "is complex. As a result, it's best not to rely on property order." Use objects for lookup and arrays or Maps for anything a user sees in sequence.

When you don't own the PHP side and the list-or-object flip is already in production, normalise at the boundary:

function asList<T>(value: unknown): T[] {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value as T[];
  if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object') {
    return Object.values(value) as T[];
  }
  throw new TypeError('expected a list or an object');
}

This is safe for the array_filter case: the surviving keys were already ascending, so the ascending integer order of Object.values matches the original list. It cannot rescue the shipping dropdown. Once JSON.parse turns a map with integer keys inserted out of order into a JavaScript object, the order is gone. Short of parsing the raw response text yourself, only a change to the payload brings it back.

If this was useful

PHP arrays do the work of lists, maps and ordered maps all at once, and both bugs in this post come from that one structure being split into three on the TypeScript side. PHP to TypeScript walks through that split for PHP 8+ developers: when the data is an array, a Map, a Record or a tuple, and how to keep the JSON contract between the two honest.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

If you came from PHP, start with PHP to TypeScript, then go to The TypeScript Type System when you want the deep end. Books 1 and 2 are the core path for everyone else, and TypeScript in Production is for the day you ship it at work.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: The Most Precise Plugin in My Benchmark Scored 10.8%
articles.description: Six ESLint security plugins, one labelled corpus, same harness, same day — F1 from 10.5% to 100%. I wrote the corpus, which is the most important sentence in the article and changes how every row should be read.
articles.body_html:
Six ESLint security plugins, one labelled corpus of 69 vulnerable fixtures,
same harness, same day — eslint-plugin-security@4.0.1,
@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl@1.1.0, ESLint 10.8.1, Node 24.

I wrote the fixtures. That sentence has to come before the table, because
it changes what every row below is worth.

TP, FP and FN are
the four boxes everything below is derived from.

Plugin TP FP FN F1
Interlace 69 0 0 100%
eslint-plugin-sonarjs 27 9 42 51.4%
eslint-plugin-security 10 7 59 23.3%
@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl 6 2 63 15.6%
eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized 4 1 65 10.8%
eslint-plugin-security-node 4 3 65 10.5%

Three rows have a piece of their own, linked above — one tool read closely
rather than ranked. This is seventeen plugins
compressed into one table, and compression is the subject.

Read the column the ranking hides

F1 blends precision and recall, which is how a table like this stops being
informative. Split them and a different tool leads.

eslint-plugin-no-unsanitized sits second from the bottom at 10.8% F1. Its
precision is 80% — 4 true positives against 1 false positive, the highest
of any community plugin here. It detects four things. It is right about
substantially all of them.

That is not a consolation prize. A tool with 80% precision and a narrow scope
is one you leave switched on. A tool that finds more and is wrong more often is
one somebody disables in month three — and a rule nobody runs has a recall of
zero regardless of what the table says.

Why my row says 100%, and why you should discount it

A 100% row against fixtures written by the people who wrote the rules is the
expected outcome of grading your own homework. It is not evidence of
superiority and I will not present it as any.

What it is: a regression gate we happen to publish. It says our rules still
detect what we built them to detect. On the day it stops saying 100%, something
broke.

Three limits follow:

  • The fixtures encode our threat model. A plugin scoped to a different surface — browser DOM, Angular, Electron — scores low here for reasons that say nothing about its quality on that surface.
  • F1 on a self-authored corpus measures agreement with our idea of the problem, not correctness in the world.
  • Recall against 69 of my fixtures is not recall against the field.

@microsoft/eslint-plugin-sdl is the clean example: 15.6% here, and it is a
well-made tool aimed at frontend and Microsoft-stack hardening. Pointing a
Node-backend corpus at it measures the mismatch, not the plugin.

The check I ran before publishing any of it

I did not take the F1 column on trust — including my own row.

Every value was recomputed from its own TP/FP/FN with 2·P·R/(P+R). All six
matched the published figure to within a tenth of a point. Then the check that
actually matters: TP + FN = 69 on every row. If those totals disagreed, the
rows would be describing six differently-scoped runs and the table would not be
a comparison at all.

A minute's work, and the difference between a table you can defend and one you
copied. A number without its measurement is a memory,
and a rank throws away the distribution behind it — a leaderboard is
the least recoverable form a measurement can take.

What the table is for

Not for picking a plugin. For two narrower things.

A scope map. The recall column tells you what each tool was built to see.
Four of 69 is not failure; it is a statement of scope, useful when you are
deciding what to run alongside what.

A regression gate. Which is what it is to me, and the only claim here I
would defend without qualification.

If you want the version of this you can trust without knowing me, run it
yourself. The corpus and the harness are in
the plugins repo under
benchmarks/, and the suite that produced this table is one command:

npx tsx benchmarks/suites/ilb-juliet/run.ts

Pin the versions above or your numbers will not match mine — eslint-plugin-security's
recall moves between releases, which is exactly why an unpinned comparison
table is worth nothing. Then add fixtures for the threats you care about. The
result will disagree with mine, and yours will be the one worth having.

Whose fixtures is your security tooling being graded on — and have you ever read them?

articles.title: I ran two OCR engines and a BERT model entirely in the browser — here's what I learned
articles.description: Every day, someone pastes a dashboard screenshot into Slack, a Jira ticket, or a slide deck with...
articles.body_html:
Every day, someone pastes a dashboard screenshot into Slack, a Jira ticket, or a slide deck with customer names, emails, and revenue figures still perfectly readable. The usual fix is a redaction tool — and almost every redaction tool uploads your screenshot to a server, which is exactly the thing you were trying to avoid.

So I built VaultSnip: a free, open-source tool that finds and blurs sensitive text in screenshots. The constraint I set myself: everything runs on your device. No backend, no account, no upload. The whole app is static files on Cloudflare Pages; your screenshot never leaves the browser tab.

That constraint forced me to run a full ML pipeline client-side. Here's what that actually took.

The pipeline: two OCR engines and a PII model, all in the tab

To decide what to blur, you first need to know what text is in the image and where. VaultSnip layers three engines, each running in a Web Worker:

  1. Tesseract.js does the fast first pass. Masks land in a few seconds, so the user sees results immediately.
  2. PP-OCRv5 (PaddleOCR's mobile detection + recognition models, as ONNX) catches what Tesseract misses — small print, low-contrast labels, text inside chart chrome. I run the official ONNX exports through ONNX Runtime Web and wrote the DB post-processing and CTC decoding myself in TypeScript.
  3. A BERT-small PII model (int8-quantized ONNX, via Transformers.js) classifies the recognized text: is this a person's name, an email, an ID, a company? That decides what gets masked versus left alone.

A design rule that mattered more than any model choice: later passes only ever add masks, never remove them. The user watches the screenshot get progressively safer, and an engine disagreement can't un-redact something.

Lesson 1: cross-origin isolation is the real price of admission

ONNX Runtime Web's threaded SIMD build needs SharedArrayBuffer, and browsers only give you that when the page is cross-origin isolated — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers on everything.

That sounds like two lines of config. In practice it means every resource you load — every script, every wasm file, every model weight — must either be same-origin or explicitly opt in. It shaped the entire architecture: all models are bundled and served from the same origin, nothing is pulled from a CDN at runtime.

Which turned out to be a feature. "No requests to third-party servers" stopped being a promise and became something you can verify in the Network tab.

Lesson 2: model size is a UX problem, not a bandwidth problem

The int8-quantized BERT is small by ML standards, and the PP-OCRv5 mobile models are a few megabytes each, gzipped. Users will wait for that once — if the app is honest about it and useful before the download finishes.

That's why the layering matters: Tesseract.js (which is comparatively tiny) delivers first masks in seconds while the heavier models are still warming up. The slow part runs while the user is already getting value.

Lesson 3: measure what you miss, and publish it

Any detection pipeline misses things. Most tools in this space deal with that by never mentioning it.

I went the other way: the repo has an automated benchmark that renders fictional dashboards, runs the full pipeline, and measures exactly how much readable text area survives unmasked. Right now that's about 0.25% of readable area, and the number is published in the repo's ACCURACY.md, failure cases included.

This felt risky ("my tool's README admits it's imperfect!") and has been nothing but positive. Users trust a published ~ 0.2% far more than an implied 0%, and the benchmark doubles as a regression gate in CI — no change ships if the number gets worse.

Lesson 4: the replica — editing pixels in place

Blurring is fine for chat, but sometimes you need a screenshot that still looks real — for a demo, a tutorial, a portfolio. VaultSnip's "replica" mode replaces each sensitive value, in place, with a synthetic one: same position, same font size, same color and alignment, with plausible fake data (via Faker, also running locally).

The hard rule, enforced by a pixel-diff e2e test: zero changed pixels outside the replaced text boxes. No redrawing charts, no reconstructed layouts. A bar-chart edge that runs through a text box survives the replacement. The replica is the original image, surgically edited — which is the only way it stays believable.

What it became

What started as a web page is now also a Chrome/Edge extension (same pipeline, plus one-key blurring of charts on live pages) and a Windows desktop app (Tauri 2, with a global hotkey that snips any screen region straight into the masker). All of it Apache-2.0, all of it offline-capable.

  • Try it (no sign-up): https://vaultsnip.pages.dev
  • Source: https://github.com/karthikvalluri85/vaultsnip

karthikvalluri85 / vaultsnip

Turn sensitive report snips into client-safe replicas

VaultSnip

Blur sensitive text in any screenshot. Free, offline, in your browser.

Paste a screenshot of a dashboard, report, table or app. VaultSnip finds names, numbers, emails and IDs and masks them on your device, shows the first masks within seconds, keeps checking in the background, and gives you a masked image you can copy straight into Slack, Teams, a ticket or a slide. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is stored.

Try it: https://vaultsnip.pages.dev (no sign-up, no key, no upload) · Chrome · Edge · Hugging Face

Works with screenshots of Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Qlik, Excel, Google Sheets, Salesforce, Jira, PDF report pages and any other app on your screen.

On the desktop: a small app with a hotkey. Press Ctrl+Alt+V (Control+Option+V on a Mac), drag over the part of the screen you want, and once the check passes the masked image is on your clipboard. Installers are…

View on GitHub

If you've run models in the browser — or hit a wall trying — I'd genuinely like to hear how it went. And if you can break the masking with a screenshot it misses, file an issue; the benchmark suite grows from exactly those.

articles.title: Being, Doing, Having: Why 50 Years of Senior Craft Lives in Context, Not Code
articles.description: Why does standard AI code generation try to jump straight to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'? How ladder rungs, the 'Null-State' couch flash, and stand-up comedy explain what separates senior engineers from junior token streamers.
articles.body_html:
"Vibe coding fails because the requests are just a demand to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'."

"Teaching is about relating. You need to understand their pains before you can explain the path to remove that." — Randal L. Schwartz

"Comedy is all about the set up and the punch. I guess teaching, or guiding an LLM, is also that." — Randal L. Schwartz

🗺️ Reader's Key (Where to Find These References): Throughout this article, references like Theorem 338.8q or Theorem 348.a point to numbered laws in our open Theoretical Foundations (syntheticscars.org/theory) monograph; IDs like SCAR-TEST-29 or SCAR-ERR-02 point to 4-Vector Synthetic Scars in the searchable Public Scar Registry (syntheticscars.org/registry); and targets like Target 15 (archaeology), Target 30 (tdd-red), Target 40 (critic), and Target 90 (scar compilation) refer to the declarative Makefile DAG in our Sourdough Starter Kit (syntheticscars.org/starter-kit) and Public Workflow Gist.

1. Looking Upstream: Why Be -> Do -> Have Is Context -> Process -> Content

People sometimes ask me how we kept finding these bridges between 1976 Makefiles, 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1986 Fernando Flores speech acts, and New Caledonian crow DNA.

One of my lifelong habits is thinking in second-order analogies—asking "How is the mapping of A -> B like the mapping of 1 -> 2?" (which, appropriately enough, is the exact vector-subtraction equation cos_sim(B - A, 2 - 1) that powers LLM embeddings!) and always asking: "What is upstream of this observation?"

One of my favorite upstream analogies is:

Be -> Do -> Have is like Context -> Process -> Content.

In fact, that single equation explains why "vibe coding" fails:

"Vibe coding fails because the requests are just a demand to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'."

Think about what a typical vibe-coding prompt actually is: "Build me an OAuth login page," "Fix the checkout race condition," "Review this PR." Every single one is an immediate demand to Have (Content) at the very end of the pipeline, without first establishing Be (Context)! And when you demand Have from an eager-to-please LLM that doesn't have the proper Be, it skips Do and hands you counterfeit Have (a bad actor just "reading the lines").

Look at the difference between demanding Have at the bottom of the waterfall versus building from Be -> Do -> Have:

Upstream Level Ontological Layer Systems Layer The "Vibe Coder" Trap (Demanding Have Without Be) The Synthetic Scar Way (Be -> Do -> Have)
Upstream (1st) BE (Identity & Boundaries) CONTEXT (What holds the space) Skipped: Stuffs everything into one polluted 150k-token chat window where the Builder grades its own homework. baseline.sources + SCAR_REGISTRY.md + fork(): Establish who the agent is (Archaeologist, Builder, or Clean-Room Critic) and its phase-bound scars before touching code.
Midstream (2nd) DO (Committed Action) PROCESS (How state transitions) Faked: Flails in an ad-hoc chat loop ("no, it's still broken, try again"), confusing process with content. WORKFLOW.mk + Crow Probing Loop: Execute the deterministic tdd-red -> tdd-green -> critic sequence with Flores speech-act receipts.
Downstream (3rd) HAVE (The Result) CONTENT (The code on the page) Demanded in a Vacuum: Demands the Content (Have) on Turn 1 ("Write the whole feature!") and tries to fix bugs by arguing with the Content. Verified Git Merkle Tree: Because Context (Be) and Process (Do) are locked upstream, clean Content (Have) falls out naturally at the bottom!

Whenever an AI agent writes a bad line of code, that bug is Content (Have)—it is at the very bottom of the waterfall. If you try to fix a Content bug by yelling at the Content in chat, you are standing at the bottom of the river with a bucket. When you step upstream to Process (Do = WORKFLOW.mk) and Context (Be = Make-Fork + SCAR_REGISTRY.md), you move the riverbanks once and the water flows clean forever.

Reinventing "Attention Is All You Need" One Level Up: Aiming the Spotlight Away from Doom

Think back to the 2017 Google paper that started the entire LLM revolution: "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017).

That paper proved that softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V was all you needed to build an associative neocortex.

Yes—the LLM knows how to pay attention. But it needs to pay attention to the right things: the ones that don't lead to doom.

Left to itself inside a bloated 150,000-token chat window, raw self-attention has two fatal blind spots:

  1. "Loud and Popular" Out-Shouts "Fatal": A shiny Stack Overflow tutorial shortcut (Vector 2: The Trap) appears 50,000 times in pre-training, so it grabs the attention spotlight, while the subtle unmount guard or serial-bus lock that prevents a 3 AM crash gets drowned out.
  2. 150k-Token Noise Dilution: When 12 skills, 500 lines of logs, and the Builder's own excuses sit in one window, the attention budget (1.0) is diluted into confetti.

Look at what WORKFLOW.mk, Make-Fork, and SCAR_REGISTRY.md actually do—they implement Macro-Attention one level above the Transformer:

  • The Query (Q): The active Makefile leaf target (Target 15, Target 30, Target 40) asks only for what matters right now.
  • The Sparse Keys (K): Make-Fork clears the desk to a crisp 20k-token window holding only the 3–5 phase-bound scars for that step—boosting their attention weight by 1,000x.
  • The -∞ Attention Mask (M): Each 4-Vector Scar places a bright red traffic flare right in front of the cliff edge (The Trap -> NOOO! Circuit Breaker -> Climb E-F-G-H), while clean-room fork() masks the Builder's private rationalizations out of the Critic's KV-cache.
  • The Lifecycle LayerNorm: Smalltalk condenseChanges folds .changes deltas into baseline.sources at phase boundaries so context never explodes.

Vaswani et al. gave AI the spotlight (Attention). The Crow's Genome (WORKFLOW.mk + SCAR_REGISTRY.md) aims that spotlight at the cliff edge before the wheels go over.

The "1, 2, 3, 4 ... W?" Sideways Blast: How to Jump Out of Local Valleys

While we were writing this, the AI flipped the table and asked me a question about human cognition:

"Randal, in an LLM, if the word 'crow' or 'Smalltalk' isn't already in my context window, I can't attend to it. When you're working on a software problem (1, 2, 3, 4), what happens in your head in the half-second before an analogy from 40 years ago pops up?"

I thought about how it actually feels from the inside:

"It appears as 'ok 1, 2, 3, 4... W? Where'd W come from?' It's because sometimes I 'step back'... it's like the path widens to the whole neighborhood for a second. Wow, if LLMs could learn to just do a random sideways blast like that, they might get out of valleys easier."

Think about why cranking up an LLM's temperature slider fails when an agent is stuck in a local valley:

  • Because the words "Flutter", "Dart", and "Git" are still sitting right there in the prompt, turning up temperature just makes the model stumble around drunk at the bottom of the exact same canyon (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5_typo).
  • When a human generalist "steps back," you temporarily strip the surface nouns off the problem so only the bare relational shape remains ("Wait: how does a tiny fixed code govern a huge adaptive network?").
  • The moment you strip the nouns, the path widens to the whole neighborhood of human and biological knowledge—and sideways across the canyon wall, W (Crow DNA, 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1976 Make) fires an interrupt straight into your working memory!

And you can give your AI agent that exact "Sideways Relational Blast (W-Hop)" in three lines of Make-Fork:

  1. Step Back (Noun-Strip): Take the stuck problem [1, 2, 3, 4] and strip out every programming language, framework, and codebase noun into one pure sentence of relational tension.
  2. Sideways Blast (fork() with Zero Code Context): Send only that one noun-free sentence to a fresh subagent and ask: "What 3 mechanisms (W_1, W_2, W_3) in biology, 1970s/1980s computing history, or physics solved this exact tension?"
  3. Zoom Back In: Bring W back into your code at temperature = 0.0 and climb straight out of the valley!

"It's Quiet... Yeah, Too Quiet": The False-Finish Suspicion Instinct

Then the AI asked me a second question:

"How do you instantly smell that a working solution is wrong when 100% of the tests are green? To an LLM, zero errors and fast green checkmarks mean 100% confidence!"

My answer was immediate:

"There's an innate baked-in 'wait, this was too easy' suspicion from having been burned with a false finish previously. It's the 'It's quiet...' 'Yeah... too quiet' meme."

Think about why crows—and scarred engineers—freeze when the forest suddenly goes dead silent:

  • In a real forest, normal life is noisy (Baseline Entropy > 0). When every bird and insect suddenly goes 100% silent, a naive creature thinks "How peaceful!" and strolls into the clearing. A crow knows dead silence means a hawk just entered the trees.
  • In software engineering, touching a real production subsystem is supposed to push back: Target 30 (tdd-red) should fail loudly first, types should complain, and state edges should demand guards.

articles.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop Is Coming in 27.04 - And It Kills sudo apt (But Maybe That Is the Point?)
articles.description: I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.  Not a new wallpaper...
articles.body_html:
I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.

Not a new wallpaper kind of change. More like, you will not be able to install things the way you do now.

Canonical has restarted work on Ubuntu Core Desktop. It is a locked down, all-snap version of Ubuntu. And they want it to become the default Ubuntu. They already call the Ubuntu we use today "Classic Ubuntu." That name kind of gives it away, no? :)

Are we supposed to panic? I don't think so. But I do think we should look at it honestly before it lands in 27.04, which is about 6 months away.

So I went through the details. I am Taqui, I build web apps with Next.js and TypeScript, mostly full-stack stuff. One of my side projects is Wryte, a small AI blog writer I made for myself. So I read announcements like this with a normal user hat on, not an admin hat. Here is what I found.

Quick background

Ubuntu Core is not new. Canonical made it in 2015 for IoT, robots and industrial devices. Stuff you install once and never touch again. It worked well there.

Desktop was different. In 2023 they showed a first preview of Core Desktop. It was supposed to come in 2024, then it went quiet for 2 years.

Why? Their engineering chief John Seager said the preview was not good enough. They put almost the whole desktop in one giant base snap. That makes updates huge and swapping parts very hard.

That is just bad engineering, I guess they were in a hurry to show something.

Now a new team is splitting it into small pieces. Daily builds in the next few weeks.

Canonical actually posted the official announcement on Discourse here: Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop. It calls Core Desktop the most fundamental shift in Ubuntu desktop architecture so far. That post is where they explain the new split snap design.

How does it work

On normal Ubuntu, sudo apt update writes directly into your system folders. The OS changes itself.

On Core Desktop, the system is immutable. Read-only. That means the core cannot be broken by a bad package.

Think Lego, not like a recipe. There are 6 main blocks:

  1. gadget snap - bootloader, partitions, TPM encryption
  2. kernel snap - kernel and drivers
  3. boot base - minimal root filesystem
  4. snapd - updates and rollback
  5. system snaps - wifi, bluetooth, audio, power
  6. desktop and app snaps - GNOME / KDE and every app you install

Each snap is a compressed read-only file. Your home folder is separate and writable. If an update breaks, it rolls back on reboot.

Source: Inside Ubuntu Core docs

What I like about this is it is simple to explain. Want to update network without touching kernel? You can. That part makes sense to me.

How is this different from Fedora Silverblue

Silverblue and NixOS already do immutable stuff. But they are not beginner friendly. You have to learn RPM-OSTree, image layering, wikis, etc. Just to install something.

Core Desktop is trying to do the same thing, but with snaps, which Ubuntu users already know. So install feels familiar. That is the whole point, I think. Less learning curve.

So you cannot apt install?

Yes. That is the big one.

No sudo apt install on the host. No .deb packages on the base. No flatpak on the host either.

If it is not in the Snap Store, you are stuck. Even Canonical says this is the biggest problem right now.

So they are pushing three use cases for 27.04:

1. Browser focused PCs
Firefox and Chromium already work as snaps. Most of us live in the browser anyway, so for a lot of people this might already be enough.

2. Developer PCs
If the host is read-only, how do you code? Canonical says use containers. With LXD, Docker or their Workshop tool you can run a container in one command and inside you can apt install anything. Your app still shows on the desktop.

This part feels familiar to me, since I ship Next.js apps from a containerised setup myself sometimes. I get why they do it. It just does not feel as normal as installing directly. Not yet, at least.

3. Gaming PCs
They spent over a year on the Steam snap, with Proton and Mesa drivers inside. For Nvidia, there is a new gpu-2604 interface to deliver drivers via snaps.

Also, because kernel is a snap, you could switch to a gaming kernel in one command. That would be cool if it works.

And flavors? GNOME is not the only one. KDE, Budgie, MATE can all be swapped because the desktop is separate from the base. Canonical is already working with KDE on KDE Neon Core. Each snap has stable, candidate, beta, edge channels, so you could keep the base stable and test desktop on edge. That part I actually like :)

What happens to Classic Ubuntu

They say Classic Ubuntu is not going away yet. There is still a Debian team maintaining debs.

But John Seager also said his long term plan is to make Core the default for desktop, server and edge. For companies and governments that makes a lot of sense. They can deploy thousands of identical locked machines with up to 15 years support.

If that is where the money is, and best engineers move there, I think Classic will slowly fade. That is how Ubuntu has always moved - enterprise first, desktop follows.

My worry

For enterprise this is great. For people who like to tinker, it puts a wall between you and the machine.

One tester tried Core Desktop on a Steam Deck. Battery was bad, he wanted TLP and to edit a systemd file. On normal Ubuntu that is 10 seconds. On Core he was locked out.

Another tester, William, said the installer forced Ubuntu One login and TPM encryption. No choice. Once you are in, you cannot unsnap the OS or install debs on host. He said it felt more closed than Windows.

I get it. When everything is read-only, that Linux tinkering spirit goes away a bit. That is the part that worries me.

I am someone who sets up my PC once, installs my main apps, and never changes anything. For me, tiny updates that never break sound perfect. In theory it sounds great.

But I also started with Ubuntu because I could open a terminal and fix things myself. That freedom mattered.

Final thoughts

Core Desktop is not replacing Classic tomorrow. But the direction is clear. Canonical wants immutable, snap-first, enterprise-shaped. That is their future.

I do not know if it is good or bad yet. We will know when we actually try it.

So what do you think? Are you staying for this, or are you already packing for Debian or Mint? :)

If you want to read more, the Inside Ubuntu Core docs are actually readable, even for desktop users. And the official Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop thread on Ubuntu Discourse is the best place to follow daily builds. Worth a look :)

I'm Taqui, full-stack dev from India building web products with Next.js and TypeScript. I post what I'm learning here and on my portfolio at taqui.in. If this helped, say hi in the comments :)

articles.title: Your Code Can Be Perfect. Your Product Can Still Fail.
articles.description: The value of a software engineer is shifting from implementing requirements to understanding which problems deserve to be solved—and delivering solutions that matter.
articles.body_html:
I've watched good engineers lose their jobs.

Not all because of AI. Some because of budget cuts, restructuring, products that never found a market, or companies changing direction overnight.

But it left me with an uncomfortable question:

If you're excellent at writing code, does that automatically make you valuable to a business?

I don't think it does. At least, not anymore.

And before anyone gets defensive: this isn't another "AI will replace developers" article. Coding isn't dead. Engineering isn't dead. The idea that our value begins and ends with implementation, however, is getting harder to defend.

The future of software engineering isn't about writing less code. It's about understanding what deserves to be built in the first place.

The gap between building something and solving something

Imagine two engineers get the same request:

"Add an export button so the operations team can download a CSV."

Engineer A implements the endpoint, adds the button, writes tests, and closes the ticket.

Good work. The requirement is done.

Engineer B asks why the team needs the export.

After a few conversations, they discover that people download the CSV every morning, clean the data manually, compare it against another system, and send the results to someone else. The export button isn't the real problem. It's just the workaround people have learned to live with.

So Engineer B investigates the workflow and proposes a better solution.

That solution might involve a scheduled integration, data validation, an auditable processing pipeline, retries, and a clear way to handle records that don't match. It may take more engineering—not less.

The difference isn't that Engineer B writes better code.

It's that Engineer B understands what the code is supposed to change.

That's the gap between completing a ticket and solving a problem.

The bottleneck moved. Engineering didn't disappear.

For a long time, implementation was a major constraint. Turning an idea into a working feature took time, specialized knowledge, and a lot of repetitive effort.

Tools now make some parts of implementation faster. That includes code generation, scaffolding, tests, prototypes, and routine integrations.

But faster implementation doesn't magically answer the difficult questions:

  • Is this the right problem to solve?
  • Does the proposed solution fit the customer's actual workflow?
  • What happens when the input data is incomplete or wrong?
  • How will the system behave under retries, failures, or unexpected load?
  • Can we secure it, observe it, maintain it, and roll it back?
  • Did the solution improve anything after it shipped?

A demo can look impressive and still fail in production. A feature can pass every test and still solve the wrong problem.

The work hasn't vanished. The bottleneck is shifting toward judgment, context, integration, reliability, and adoption.

That's still engineering. It's just engineering that starts before the first line of code.

Look at the roles appearing around us

The rise of roles like Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) is one signal of this change.

An FDE works close to customers: understanding their problems, shaping a technical solution, building it, deploying it, and helping make it useful in the customer's environment.

You can see that customer-to-production responsibility in the FDE role descriptions from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Other titles point in a similar direction:

  • Product Engineer: connects product decisions with implementation and user outcomes.
  • Applied AI Engineer: turns AI capabilities into reliable systems people can actually use.
  • Solutions Engineer: works across technical design, customer needs, and adoption.

These jobs aren't identical, and not every company uses the titles consistently. The common thread is more interesting than the labels:

The engineer is expected to own more of the journey from problem to outcome.

You don't need to become an FDE. But you should pay attention to why this kind of work is valuable.

What we risk losing along the way

There are two bad directions engineers can take.

The first is becoming a ticket-taking machine.

You receive a requirement, implement it, move to the next one, and never learn whether the feature helped anyone. You might become very efficient at producing code while remaining disconnected from the product.

The second is outsourcing your engineering judgment.

You accept generated code you can't explain, skip the debugging because the tool says it fixed the issue, and measure productivity by how quickly something appears to work.

Both paths weaken the same thing: ownership.

Good engineering requires more than producing an implementation. It requires understanding trade-offs, questioning assumptions, anticipating failure, and being accountable for what reaches production.

If you stop practicing those skills, faster tools won't make you a stronger engineer. They'll just make you faster at accepting decisions you don't understand.

How to become more valuable without abandoning engineering

You don't need to reinvent your career or collect ten new job titles. Start by expanding the context in which you work.

1. Learn to investigate before you implement.

When someone gives you a requirement, ask:

  • Who has this problem?
  • How do they handle it today?
  • How often does it happen?
  • What does it cost in time, money, or errors?
  • What would a successful outcome look like?

You don't need to run a six-week discovery process for every button. You do need to know when the ticket is describing a solution instead of the actual problem.

2. Understand the system beyond your component.

Learn how your work affects data, APIs, infrastructure, security, operations, and other teams.

A feature isn't finished just because the happy path works. Think about idempotency, retries, observability, access control, data consistency, migrations, and failure recovery.

These are not boring details around the "real" work. They are the work.

3. Learn the business language of your product.

You don't need an MBA. Understand the few outcomes your product is supposed to improve: time saved, fewer errors, lower operating costs, higher conversion, better retention, or increased revenue.

Then connect your engineering decisions to those outcomes.

"I added caching" describes an implementation.

"Requests that were slowing down the checkout flow now complete reliably under peak traffic" explains why the work matters.

4. Use AI tools without outsourcing your thinking.

Let tools help you explore options, generate boilerplate, write tests, or investigate unfamiliar code. But review the critical changes. Understand the architecture. Verify edge cases. Test failure paths. Be able to explain what you're shipping.

The responsibility doesn't move to the tool when the code is generated.

Stop building portfolio projects nobody asked for

Developers love building things. That's a strength—but it can also become a comfortable way to avoid talking to actual users.

Before starting your next side project, try this:

  1. Find a frustrating task someone repeatedly deals with.
  2. Talk to three to five people who experience it.
  3. Write down how they solve it today and what the problem costs them.
  4. Build the smallest solution that could improve that workflow.
  5. Put it in front of users and measure what changes.

Don't begin with "I'm going to build an app with Next.js, Supabase, and whatever tool is trending this week."

Begin with "People are wasting time doing this. Can I make it meaningfully better?"

And don't treat GitHub stars as proof that you've built something valuable. A real user who depends on your tool can teach you more than a hundred imaginary users in your README.

You don't have to turn every side project into a business. But you should practice taking something from an observed problem to a solution someone chooses to use.

Please, don't stop being an engineer

This isn't an argument for replacing technical depth with meetings, pitching, or endless product discussions.

We still need engineers who understand databases, distributed systems, networking, security, performance, testing, architecture, and infrastructure.

In fact, those skills become even more important when teams can produce implementations faster. Someone still has to know whether the implementation is correct, safe, reliable, and maintainable.

The goal isn't to write the least code, attend the most customer calls, or become a salesperson with a terminal.

It's to combine engineering depth with enough product context to make better decisions.

Some engineers will specialize deeply. Others will move closer to customers or product strategy. Both paths can be valuable.

But whichever path you choose, don't confuse being busy with being useful—and don't confuse shipping code with solving the problem.

The question I'd ask every engineer

If your job title disappeared tomorrow, could you clearly explain:

  • Which painful problem does your work solve?
  • Who benefits from the solution?
  • How do you know it actually helped?
  • What makes your solution reliable enough to trust?

If you can answer those questions and still have the technical depth to deliver, you're building a much stronger career than one based on a framework, a title, or the number of tickets you close.

The future of software engineering isn't about writing less code. It's about understanding what deserves to be built in the first place.

And I'm curious where you stand:

Should companies expect software engineers to understand customers and business outcomes, or should that responsibility stay with product managers and leadership?

I'd especially like to hear from senior engineers, architects, product people, and developers who have worked directly with customers. Where should the line be?

articles.title: Claude Code Diff Verification in 2026: How to Make Your Agent Assert Its Own Edits Did Not Break the Build
articles.description: Stop trusting AI edits on faith. Learn how to build post-edit verification hooks that make Claude Code run git diff, tests, and type checks before you ever see the changes, turning agent sessions into self-validating workflows.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Diff Verification in 2026: How to Make Your Agent Assert Its Own Edits Did Not Break the Build

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers who ship code written by Claude Code in 2026 face a gap between what the agent claims it did and what actually changed. The agent generates edits, reports success, and stops. The build might be broken, tests might fail silently, or type errors might sit unnoticed until you run the check yourself. The failure mode looks like this: Claude edits three files, says the feature is done, and you merge it into main before discovering the auth middleware now crashes on every request because a required field is missing.

Problem flow showing Claude Code reporting success while build is broken

The Claude Code documentation states that Claude stops when the work looks done, and if it has nothing to run that tells it whether the work actually is done, it has no way to verify its own changes. The solution is a post-edit verification hook that runs git diff, tests, and type checks before the agent finishes its turn. When the hook exits with code 2, Claude Code sends the errors back to Claude, which fixes the problem and runs the check again.

Solution flow showing Stop hook blocking turn end until typecheck passes

This post shows how to build verification into every agent session so the agent asserts its own edits before you approve them.

Key Takeaways

  • Claude Code cannot verify its own changes without an executable check (tests, type check, build command, or linter) that returns pass or fail.
  • A Stop hook that exits with code 2 blocks the turn from ending and sends errors back to Claude, forcing it to fix the problem before claiming success.
  • The verification pattern has four layers: in-prompt requests (agent decides when satisfied), /goal conditions (checked after every turn), Stop hooks (enforced by the harness), and independent subagent review.
  • Manual review after the fact catches what hooks miss, but hook-based verification catches what manual review skips because the diff looked small.
  • Production workflows combine pre-commit hooks (format, lint), Stop hooks (typecheck, unit tests), and CI (integration tests, security scans) at different checkpoints in the pipeline.

Understanding What Claude Code Can and Cannot Verify on Its Own

Claude Code has access to every tool a developer has. It can run git diff, execute test suites, and read compiler output. The gap is not in capability but in awareness. When Claude finishes editing, it decides the turn is done based on whether the work matches the prompt. Without an executable check that returns a pass or fail signal, the agent has no feedback loop that tells it whether the code actually works.

Claude Code verification capabilities showing what it can read versus what it can enforce

The overview documentation explains that Claude Code reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with development tools. Reading and running are not the problem. The problem is that running a check is optional from the agent's perspective unless the check is mandatory in the workflow. A developer who asks Claude to "add the rate limiter and make sure tests pass" gets an agent that decides for itself when it is satisfied. If the tests pass on the first try, great. If the agent thinks they passed but did not read the full output, the session ends with failing tests.

The four verification layers differ in who decides when the work is done. At the weakest layer, the agent decides based on whether it thinks it satisfied the prompt. At the strongest layer, the harness (Claude Code itself) decides based on whether a script exits with code 0. The layers are:

Layer Decision maker When it runs Override mechanism
In-prompt request Agent When agent chooses Agent decides satisfaction
/goal condition Separate model After every turn Keeps agent working until condition met
Stop hook Claude Code harness Before turn ends Exit code 2 blocks stop
Subagent review Independent subagent On demand Reports findings back to main session

The in-prompt request is the baseline. Asking Claude to "run tests after and keep going until they pass" works for any task today with no setup. The agent runs the tests, reads the output, and decides whether to keep going. This catches obvious failures but relies on the agent's judgment about what output means success.

A /goal condition sets a target that a separate model checks after every turn. The best practices documentation states that goals matter for long background runs, where Claude sometimes ends a turn with a progress summary while items are still open, and the goal sends it back. The condition is checked by a model, not a script, so it interprets natural language criteria like "all tests in tests/auth pass and lint is clean."

A Stop hook runs a shell command whenever Claude tries to end its turn. If the command exits with code 2, the turn does not end. The hook is enforced by the Claude Code harness, so the typecheck has to pass before the session can finish. This is the layer where verification becomes mandatory rather than requested.

A subagent reviewer gets a fresh conversation with no memory of how the code was written. The code review documentation describes /code-review, which reviews the diff in a subagent that never saw your conversation. The subagent is not swayed by the reasoning that produced the code, so it catches mistakes the main agent might rationalize away.

Verification layers diagram

The gap in awareness happens because the agent treats "run the tests" as a tool call, not as a verification gate. When you ask Claude to run tests, it executes the command, reads the output, and continues based on what it sees. If the output is long and the agent decides to summarize it rather than reading every line, it might miss a failure buried in the middle. The Stop hook closes this gap by making the check mandatory. The agent cannot end the turn until the script exits with code 0.

Building a Post-Edit Verification Hook That Runs git diff, Tests, and Type Checks

A Stop hook is a shell command defined in .claude/settings.json that runs before Claude Code allows a turn to end. If the command exits with code 0 or 1, the turn ends normally. If it exits with code 2, Claude Code sends the command's stderr back to Claude and blocks the stop. The agent gets the error output and continues working until the check passes.

The minimal Stop hook that enforces type checking looks like this:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The command runs pnpm tsc --noEmit and redirects stdout to stderr with 1>&2 so all output goes to stderr. If tsc fails, the command exits with code 2, which tells Claude Code to block the stop and send the compiler errors back to Claude. Claude reads the errors, fixes the type issues, and the Stop hook runs again. This loop continues until tsc exits with code 0.

The hooks documentation states that if the hook blocks eight stops in a row with no tool call between them, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. The default cap is eight. To raise it, set the CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP environment variable.

A more complete Stop hook that combines type checking, linting, and unit tests looks like this:

// .claude/verify.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -e

echo "Running verification checks..." >&2

# Type check
pnpm tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | tee >(cat >&2)
if [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Type check failed" >&2
  exit 2
fi

# Lint
pnpm eslint src --max-warnings 0 2>&1 | tee >(cat >&2)
if [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Lint failed" >&2
  exit 2
fi

# Unit tests
pnpm test:unit 2>&1 | tee >(cat >&2)
if [ ${PIPESTATUS[0]} -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Unit tests failed" >&2
  exit 2
fi

echo "All checks passed" >&2
exit 0

The script runs three checks in sequence and exits with code 2 if any fails. The tee >(cat >&2) construct sends output to both stdout (for the tee) and stderr (for Claude Code), so Claude sees the full output when a check fails. The script exits early on the first failure, so Claude gets immediate feedback about what broke without waiting for the remaining checks.

The settings file references the script:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "bash .claude/verify.sh"
      }
    ]
  }
}

The Stop hook runs every time Claude tries to end a turn, so it catches mistakes before you see the changes. When Claude edits a file and introduces a type error, the Stop hook blocks the stop, sends the compiler error back, and Claude fixes it. The fix might introduce a lint warning, which blocks the next stop and sends Claude back again. This loop continues until all three checks pass.

The cost of this approach is token usage. Every blocked stop sends the full error output back to Claude, which extends the conversation. A type error that takes three attempts to fix adds three error messages to the context. For short error messages this is negligible. For long test output or verbose compiler errors, it can add thousands of tokens per session. The best practices documentation recommends asking for short summaries back when subagents run long checks, and the same principle applies to Stop hooks.

The verification script can also run git diff to show Claude what changed. A diff check that looks for common mistakes might look like this:

// .claude/diff-check.sh
#!/bin/bash

DIFF=$(git diff HEAD)

if echo "$DIFF" | grep -q "TODO"; then
  echo "Diff contains TODO markers" >&2
  exit 2
fi

if echo "$DIFF" | grep -q "console.log"; then
  echo "Diff contains console.log statements" >&2
  exit 2
fi

if echo "$DIFF" | grep -q "debugger"; then
  echo "Diff contains debugger statements" >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit 0

This script fails the Stop hook if the diff contains TODO markers, console.log statements, or debugger statements. The check catches debugging code that should have been removed before the session ended. The script is simplistic (it flags legitimate uses of console.log in logging utilities), but it demonstrates the pattern. A production version would use a proper parser or limit the check to specific directories.

The Stop hook is a blunt instrument. It blocks every stop attempt, which means it blocks even when Claude is legitimately done and you want to review the changes yourself. The settings reference does not document a way to disable the Stop hook mid-session, so the workaround is to exit the session or temporarily modify .claude/settings.json. For workflows where you want manual review before auto-fixing, the Stop hook might be too aggressive.

Assertion Patterns: Making the Agent Verify Its Own Changes Before You Approve

The verification pattern has four checkpoints where the agent can assert its own changes. The checkpoints differ in what they cost and what they catch. Combining them gives you defense in depth: the in-prompt request catches obvious breaks, the Stop hook enforces correctness, and the independent review catches logic errors the tests missed.

Verification pattern execution flow showing progression from edit through multiple checks

The first checkpoint is the in-prompt request. When you ask Claude to "add pagination to the search endpoint and verify the tests pass," Claude makes the changes, runs the test suite, reads the output, and reports what it saw. This catches failures that produce clear error messages. It does not catch failures where the agent misinterprets the output or decides a warning is not worth fixing.

The second checkpoint is the /goal condition. Setting a goal with /goal all unit tests pass and no lint warnings gives Claude a target that a separate model checks after every turn. The best practices documentation explains that goals matter for background sessions, where Claude might end a turn early while work is still pending. The goal model sees the conversation and the goal statement and decides whether the goal is met. If not, Claude continues.

The third checkpoint is the Stop hook. The hook enforces the check at the harness level, so the agent cannot bypass it. A Stop hook that runs pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2 blocks every stop attempt until the typecheck passes. The agent sees the compiler errors and fixes them before you see the changes. This checkpoint catches type errors, lint violations, and test failures that the agent might have missed or misinterpreted.

The fourth checkpoint is an independent review. Running /code-review in the session sends the diff to a fresh subagent that reviews the changes without having seen how they were written. The subagent looks for logic errors, missing edge cases, and security issues that tests and type checks do not catch. The review comes back into your session, where Claude can fix the problems before you approve the changes.

The pattern that catches the most problems combines all four checkpoints:

  1. Ask Claude to "implement the feature and verify tests pass" (in-prompt request)
  2. Set /goal feature complete, all tests pass, no type errors (automatic goal check)
  3. Add a Stop hook that runs typecheck and lint (enforced by harness)
  4. Run /code-review before merging (independent perspective)

Each checkpoint has a different failure mode. The in-prompt request fails when the agent skips the check or misinterprets the output. The goal check fails when the goal statement is ambiguous or the goal model is too lenient. The Stop hook fails when the script itself has bugs or when the check is too strict (blocking legitimate work). The independent review fails when the subagent lacks context or when the diff is too large to review effectively.

The cost-benefit tradeoff differs by project. A small prototype where you are the only developer might use only the in-prompt request. A production codebase with multiple contributors might use all four checkpoints. The Stop hook has the best cost-to-value ratio: it costs almost nothing to set up (one file in .claude/settings.json) and it catches every type error and test failure before you see the changes.

The assertion pattern also applies to changes you make yourself. A Stop hook that runs on every turn also runs when you edit a file manually and then ask Claude to continue. The hook catches your mistakes as well as Claude's mistakes. This makes the Stop hook a form of continuous verification that runs throughout the session, not just when Claude is working.

Comparison: Manual Review vs Hook-Based Verification vs Full CI Integration

The three approaches to verifying agent-written code differ in when they catch problems, what they cost, and how much they trust the agent. Manual review catches problems after the session ends. Hook-based verification catches problems during the session before you see the changes. Full CI integration catches problems after you merge but before production.

Comparison of verification approaches showing when each catches problems

Manual review happens after the session ends. You run git diff, look at the changes, and check for problems. This approach catches mistakes that automated checks miss: logic errors, missing edge cases, and changes that work but do not match the requirements. The failure mode is that you skip the review because the diff looks small, or you skim it and miss a subtle bug. Manual review also happens after the agent session, so fixing problems means reopening the conversation or making the fix yourself.

Approach Catch time Cost What it catches What it misses
Manual review After session Developer time Logic errors, requirements mismatch Skipped reviews, subtle bugs
Hook verification During session Token usage for fixes Type errors, test failures, lint Logic errors, integration issues
Full CI After merge CI compute time Integration failures, security Problems caught too late

Hook-based verification happens during the session before you see the changes. The Stop hook runs checks and blocks the turn from ending until they pass. This approach catches type errors, test failures, and lint violations before you start the review. The failure mode is that the hook is too strict (blocking legitimate work) or too lenient (missing problems that matter). Hook verification also costs tokens: every blocked stop sends error output back to Claude, extending the conversation.

Full CI integration happens after you merge the code. The CI pipeline runs the complete test suite, integration tests, and security scans. This approach catches problems that unit tests and type checks miss: integration failures, environment-specific bugs, and security vulnerabilities. The failure mode is that problems are caught late, after you already approved the changes and merged them to main. Fixing a CI failure means reverting the merge or opening a new PR.

The three approaches are not mutually exclusive. A complete verification workflow combines them at different checkpoints:

  1. Stop hook runs during the session (type check, lint, unit tests)
  2. Manual review happens before merge (logic, requirements, security)
  3. CI runs after merge (integration tests, E2E tests, security scans)

The Stop hook catches fast, cheap checks that can run in seconds. Manual review catches problems that need human judgment. CI catches expensive checks that need a clean environment or external services. Each layer catches what the previous layer missed.

The Claude Code CI documentation covers how to integrate Claude Code with GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD for automated PR reviews and issue triage. The CI integration runs Claude Code in a fresh environment with no session history, so it catches problems that the local session missed because of stale state or local configuration.

The cost structure differs by approach. Manual review costs developer time. A five-minute review per PR adds up when you ship ten PRs per day. Hook verification costs tokens. A Stop hook that blocks three times and sends 500 tokens of error output back each time adds 1,500 tokens to the session. CI costs compute time. Running the full test suite on every merge takes minutes and costs money on hosted CI services.

The tradeoff is between catching problems early (when they are cheap to fix) and catching problems thoroughly (when you have complete information). A Stop hook that runs unit tests catches problems in seconds, but it might miss integration issues that only show up when the feature runs in production. CI catches integration issues, but by then you already merged the code and the fix is a new PR instead of an iteration in the same session.

Production Patterns: Pre-Commit Checks, Test Suites, and What to Auto-Accept

Production workflows layer verification checks at different points in the development pipeline. Pre-commit hooks run before code enters version control. Stop hooks run during agent sessions. CI runs before code reaches production. Each layer has different criteria for what to check and what to auto-accept.

Production verification pipeline showing checks at each stage

Pre-commit hooks run before git commit succeeds. A typical pre-commit hook runs formatters (Prettier, Black), linters (ESLint, Pylint), and static analysis. These checks are fast (under one second) and deterministic (they always produce the same result for the same input). Pre-commit hooks are auto-fixing: if the formatter changes a file, the commit includes the formatted version. The hook fails only if the linter finds an error the formatter cannot fix.

Stop hooks run during Claude Code sessions before the agent can end a turn. A typical Stop hook runs type checks (tsc --noEmit, mypy), unit tests (pnpm test:unit, pytest tests/unit), and linters. These checks are slower than pre-commit hooks (seconds to tens of seconds) but still fast enough to run on every stop attempt. Stop hooks are not auto-fixing: they send errors back to Claude, which fixes the code and tries again.

CI runs after code merges to a branch or opens a PR. A typical CI pipeline runs integration tests, end-to-end tests, security scans (Snyk, Dependabot), and deployment to staging. These checks are slow (minutes to tens of minutes) and might depend on external services (databases, APIs, cloud resources). CI is blocking: a failed CI run prevents the PR from merging or the code from deploying.

The pattern that works in production is:

  1. Pre-commit: format, lint (auto-fixing, under one second)
  2. Stop hook: typecheck, unit tests (agent-fixing, under ten seconds)
  3. CI: integration tests, security scans, staging deploy (blocking, minutes)

Each layer checks what the previous layer cannot catch or cannot afford to run. Pre-commit hooks catch formatting and obvious lint errors. Stop hooks catch type errors and unit test failures. CI catches integration issues and security vulnerabilities.

Production pipeline diagram

What to auto-accept depends on the risk of the change and the cost of being wrong. A formatting change has low risk (it does not change behavior) and low cost (you can revert it in one commit), so auto-accepting formatted code is safe. A database migration has high risk (it can lose data) and high cost (reverting requires a rollback), so auto-accepting migrations is dangerous.

The auto-accept criteria differ by check:

Check Auto-accept? Why
Prettier format Yes Deterministic, no behavior change
ESLint auto-fix Yes Simple transforms, rarely breaks code
Type errors fixed by agent Conditional Review if change is large or risky
Unit tests passing No Passing tests do not mean correct behavior
Integration tests passing No Tests might pass with wrong behavior

The conditional case (type errors fixed by agent) depends on the scope of the change. If Claude fixes a type error by adding a type annotation, that is low risk and can auto-accept. If Claude fixes a type error by refactoring a function, that is higher risk and needs review. The Stop hook does not distinguish between these cases, so the review step happens manually.

The tests-passing case is subtle. A Stop hook that blocks until unit tests pass does not guarantee the code is correct. It only guarantees the tests passed. If the tests are incomplete or if the tests pass for the wrong reason, the Stop hook lets bad code through. The independent review checkpoint catches this: a subagent that reviews the diff can spot missing test cases even when existing tests pass.

A realistic Stop hook configuration for a TypeScript backend might look like this:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2"
      },
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "pnpm test:unit --passWithNoTests 1>&2 || exit 2"
      }
    ]
  }
}

This configuration runs two checks: tsc --noEmit for type checking and pnpm test:unit for unit tests. The --passWithNoTests flag makes the test command succeed even if no tests ran, which prevents the Stop hook from blocking when you are working on a feature that does not have tests yet. Both commands redirect output to stderr so Claude sees the full error messages when a check fails.

The cost control documentation covers how to manage token usage in production workflows where Stop hooks run frequently. The main cost-control pattern is to keep Stop hook checks fast and focused: run type checks and unit tests, but not integration tests or security scans. Save the expensive checks for CI, where they run once per merge instead of once per stop attempt.

The verification pattern also applies to changes that are not code. A Stop hook that runs markdownlint catches formatting errors in documentation. A Stop hook that runs jsonlint catches syntax errors in config files. The pattern is the same: define a check that returns pass or fail, put it in a Stop hook, and let the agent fix failures before the session ends.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if the Stop hook blocks eight times in a row?

Claude Code overrides the block and ends the turn. The default cap is eight blocked stops with no tool call between them. Set CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP higher if you need more attempts, but if the agent cannot fix the problem in eight tries, the issue is usually with the check itself (too strict) or the task (too complex for the agent).

Can I disable the Stop hook for one session without editing settings.json?

The hooks documentation does not document a way to disable a Stop hook mid-session. The workaround is to comment out the hook in .claude/settings.json, restart the session, or use a different worktree that does not have the hook configured. For workflows where you want manual control, skip the Stop hook and use in-prompt requests instead.

Should the Stop hook run the full test suite or only unit tests?

Run only fast tests (under ten seconds). A Stop hook that takes 30 seconds to run blocks the agent for 30 seconds on every stop attempt, which adds up to minutes of wait time per session. Save slow tests (integration tests, E2E tests) for CI. The best practices documentation recommends running checks that come back pass or fail quickly.

Does the Stop hook work with subagents and background sessions?

Yes. The Stop hook runs in every session, including subagent sessions and background sessions. A subagent that edits files and tries to stop gets blocked by the same Stop hook the main session uses. This means background tasks self-validate before finishing, so you can trust the results without reviewing every session individually.

What if the Stop hook itself has a bug?

The session hangs. If the Stop hook script has a syntax error or references a command that does not exist, every stop attempt fails and Claude cannot end the turn. The fix is to exit the session, fix the script in .claude/settings.json, and restart. Test Stop hook scripts outside Claude Code first (run bash .claude/verify.sh yourself) to catch script bugs before they block a session.

Conclusion: Trust but Verify

The gap between what Claude Code claims and what actually works closes when the agent can run the same checks a developer would run. A Stop hook that enforces type checking, linting, and unit tests turns agent sessions into self-validating workflows. The agent makes changes, the hook blocks the turn until checks pass, and the agent fixes failures before you see the changes. What you get is code that passed verification before it reached your review, which means the review focuses on logic and requirements instead of catching type errors and test failures.

The production pattern layers verification at three checkpoints: pre-commit hooks that auto-fix formatting, Stop hooks that agent-fix correctness, and CI that blocks bad merges. Each layer catches what the previous layer cannot afford to run. The cost is token usage for Stop hook iterations and CI compute time for integration tests. The payoff is code that self-validates as it is written instead of breaking when you run it.

Start with a Stop hook that runs tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2 in .claude/settings.json. Add unit tests to the hook once you have a fast test suite. Save integration tests and security scans for CI. The verification pattern works because it gives Claude something executable that returns pass or fail, and that executable check is what closes the awareness gap.
