articles.title: Running an NVIDIA DLSS Neural-Rendering Pipeline on Apple Silicon
articles.description: Hey everyone!  So, a few days ago, I came across a project on GitHub called MLX-DLSS, which...
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone!

So, a few days ago, I came across a project on GitHub called MLX-DLSS, which attempted to port NVIDIA's DLSS 5 technology to macOS using the MLX backend.

I was genuinely disappointed when I saw the performance numbers: 6 FPS, and that too on a pre-rendered video with just a single pass. 💀

So I decided to experiment with it myself.

Before going further, I should mention that I did take partial help from a coding agent, mainly for testing and analysis. The actual coding and implementation work was done by me.

Anyway, here's what I ended up doing.

I ported the project into OBS Studio as a plugin, extracted the model weights from nvngx_dlssnr.dll (the main Windows DLSS 5 neural-rendering DLL provided by NVIDIA), and started engineering a different, hybrid backend.

The idea was to distribute the workload across Apple's available hardware rather than relying entirely on GPU inference.

Here's how my current pipeline works:

Apple Neural Engine (ANE) via Core ML: Handles the main deep-learning transformer inference passes using the 31 HT and 71 HT models.

MLX: Handles AI upscaling and experimental frame generation.

Temporal stability: I've implemented temporal stabilization to reduce texture flickering and RGB poisoning.

A small warning about frame generation: it's still experimental, partially implemented, and quite buggy. I'm actively working on improving it.

The good news is that temporal stability has improved significantly. Texture flickering is much less noticeable, and RGB poisoning has been reduced by a huge margin compared to my earlier tests.

How am I feeding frames into the pipeline?

Right now, I'm using a PS5 connected to my Mac through an HDMI capture card, with the captured frames being processed through OBS Studio.

However, the pipeline isn't limited to PS5 footage. It can process other OBS video sources as well.

The three rendering modes

I've implemented three different modes: Fidelity, Balanced, and Performance.

  1. Fidelity Mode

This is the heaviest configuration.

It uses a double 71 HT transformer pass, prioritizing neural-rendering quality over performance.

Current results:

Without frame generation: 8–11 FPS

With frame generation: ~35 FPS

It looks impressive, but as mentioned earlier, frame generation is still experimental and can introduce visual artifacts and instability.

  1. Balanced Mode

This one is particularly interesting.

Instead of running the same model twice, Balanced uses a heterogeneous pipeline, with the first pass running the 31 HT model and the second pass running the 71 HT model.

Current results:

Without frame generation: 12.5–15 FPS

With frame generation: 45–48 FPS

It's basically my attempt to combine the advantages of both models without going all-in on the heavier double-71 configuration.

  1. Performance Mode

This is the lightweight configuration.

It runs a single 31 HT transformer pass.

Current results:

Without frame generation: ~20 FPS

With frame generation: 70–80 FPS

Obviously, there's a trade-off in rendering quality compared to Fidelity, but this mode provides considerably better performance.

Again, the frame-generated numbers shouldn't be confused with native inference performance. FG is still a work in progress, and visual stability isn't completely solved yet.

How am I even getting double-digit FPS?

Now, you might be wondering how I went from the original project's 6 FPS on a pre-rendered video to these numbers.

Well, I changed quite a few things in the original approach.

(A) The 480p neural-inference trick

Instead of directly feeding full 1080p frames into the neural inference backend, I do something different.

First, I capture the console output at 1080p through the HDMI capture card.

Then I downscale the frames to 480p before feeding them into the neural-rendering backend.

Once neural inference is complete, I upscale the output back to 1080p using an MLX-based AI upscaler.

The idea is to reduce the computational cost of inference while using AI upscaling to reconstruct and preserve details that conventional spatial or temporal upscaling might soften.

In some scenes, the resulting details can even appear better than the original input.

Of course, this approach has its own limitations, but the performance improvement has been pretty substantial.

(B) Moving neural inference from MLX to the ANE

This was another major change.

The original project relied on MLX for GPU-based neural inference.

Instead of following the same approach, I moved major parts of the deep-learning network onto Apple's Neural Engine through Core ML.

Think of it this way:

On NVIDIA GPUs, you have dedicated Tensor Cores for accelerating certain AI workloads.

On Apple Silicon, you have the Apple Neural Engine, which provides dedicated hardware acceleration for supported machine-learning operations.

They're not architecturally identical, obviously, but the general idea is to take advantage of dedicated neural acceleration hardware.

My goal was to avoid putting all the inference pressure on the GPU, especially since the GPU is already doing other work.

MLX is still useful, and newer Apple GPU architectures, particularly the M5 series and beyond, may offer additional advantages for GPU-based machine learning.

But for my M4 Pro, using Core ML to leverage the ANE for the main transformer inference stages made much more sense for this particular workload.

So instead of having MLX handle everything, I ended up with a heterogeneous backend where Core ML/ANE and MLX handle different parts of the pipeline.

Other things I've implemented

I've also recreated a RenoDX/OptiScaler-style configuration menu for DLSS 5, allowing users to tweak different model and pipeline settings.

Alongside that, I've implemented an RTSS-style performance metrics overlay to monitor performance while the pipeline is running.

These are still evolving, just like the rest of the project.

What's next?

The biggest thing I'm working on right now is frame-generation stability.

Temporal stabilization has already helped reduce flickering and RGB artifacts significantly in the normal neural-rendering pipeline, but enabling frame generation can still reintroduce some of those issues.

So that's my current priority.

The project is very much experimental, and there's still a lot of testing, optimization, and debugging left to do.

But considering where the original experiment started, I'm pretty happy with the progress so far.

GitHub repository

Here's the project:

https://github.com/Anonymous137-sudo/NVDLSS5_CML_MTL

Feel free to check it out, give it a try, and share your feedback!

I'm particularly interested in hearing from people working with Apple Silicon, Core ML, MLX, Metal, neural rendering, or similar graphics pipelines.

articles.title: A New JsonSerializerOptions Every Call Cost Me 120x
articles.description: A tiny endpoint was allocating like crazy. The culprit was a fresh JsonSerializerOptions built inside the handler on every request. Here's the measured cost and the one-line fix.
articles.body_html:
A list endpoint on one of my services started showing up heavier in the traces than it had any right to be. It pulled a small object, serialized it, returned it. The payload was tiny — an order with three line items. But under load the thing allocated like it was streaming a video, and the CPU time didn't match the shape of the work. I went looking for the expensive query. There wasn't one. The expensive part was the return.

Here's the line I'd written, more or less, inside the handler:

var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
});

Looks fine. It is not fine. That new JsonSerializerOptions { ... } sitting inside a method that runs on every request is the whole bug.

What the options object actually is

I used to think JsonSerializerOptions was a settings bag — a few flags, a naming policy, done. It isn't. The first time you serialize with a given options instance, System.Text.Json walks your type with reflection, builds the metadata it needs to write it (the contract for Order, for Line, the converters, the property names), caches all of that on that options instance, and then freezes the instance so it can't change underneath the cache. That setup is not cheap, and it's the reason the reused path is fast: you pay once, then every serialize after that rides the warm cache.

Build a new options object every call and you throw that cache away every call. Fresh reflection, fresh contracts, fresh everything, two hundred thousand times. You're not configuring a serializer. You're constructing one from scratch in your hot path.

Making it admit the cost

I didn't want to argue from a profiler's hunch, so I ran both shapes side by side. Same order, same settings, serialized 200,000 times. One path news up the options each iteration. The other builds it once and reuses it. I measured wall time and total allocated bytes for each. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio far more than the raw milliseconds.

static JsonSerializerOptions BuildOptions() => new()
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
};

var cached = BuildOptions();

// warm both paths' first-use cost before timing
_ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, cached);
_ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, BuildOptions());

// Path A: a brand-new options object on every call
var before = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++)
{
    var opts = BuildOptions();
    _ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, opts);
}
sw.Stop();
var aMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
var aAlloc = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true) - before;

// Path B: one cached instance, reused
before = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
sw.Restart();
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++)
    _ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, cached);
sw.Stop();
var bMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
var bAlloc = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true) - before;

The order itself is nothing special — a record with an enum status and a list of three lines, the kind of thing any API hands back:

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, OrderStatus Status, List<Line> Lines);
record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled }

Here's what printed, on .NET 10, Release build:

Serializing the same order 200,000 times.

new options each call : 17,402.5 ms    7,021.9 MB
one cached instance   :    146.0 ms      166.3 MB

time   : ~120x slower when rebuilt each call
memory :  ~42x more allocated

A hundred and twenty times slower. Seven gigabytes of allocation to produce the exact same JSON string that the cached path produced in a hundred and sixty-six megabytes. I ran it twice to be sure the numbers held, and they did, within a few percent. That's not a tuning opportunity. That's a serializer rebuilding its entire type model, over and over, for no reason.

The fix is embarrassingly small

Move the options out of the method. Build it once, hang it off a static field, reuse it forever.

static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOpts = new()
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
};

// in the handler
var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, JsonOpts);

That's the entire change. The instance is immutable once it's been used anyway, so sharing it across every request and every thread is exactly what it's built for — JsonSerializer reads from a frozen options object concurrently without complaint.

If your settings really do vary per call, and sometimes they genuinely do, don't fall back to newing one up each time. Cache the handful of variants you actually use, keyed by whatever differs. In practice most codebases have two or three distinct option sets total, not one per request. And if you're on the default settings with no customization at all, JsonSerializer.Serialize(order) already uses a cached internal instance, so the parameterless call was never the problem — it's specifically the configured-options-inline pattern that bites.

One honest caveat on the number: 120x is what this payload and this machine gave me. A bigger, deeper object graph makes the per-call rebuild even more lopsided because there's more metadata to reconstruct. A trivial payload narrows the gap. But I've never seen reuse lose, and the allocation story is one-directional regardless — a fresh options object is always garbage you didn't need to make.

I keep finding these in code reviews now that I know the shape. Any new JsonSerializerOptions that isn't assigned to a static readonly field is worth a second look. Nine times out of ten it's sitting in a method that runs a lot.

Where's yours hiding? Drop a line if you find one in a hot path — I'd bet money it's in a serialization helper somebody wrote once and never profiled.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to profile

articles.title: I Parsed the Same Format String Five Million Times
articles.description: string.Format reparses its template on every call. CompositeFormat parses it once, and the allocation drop is not subtle.
articles.body_html:
I had an exporter writing CSV lines, one per row, millions of rows a night. Nothing clever in it: a string.Format call with a template and three values. It was slower than it should've been, so I put a profiler on it, and the call that lit up wasn't the file write or the decimal math. It was the formatting. Specifically, it was the part of string.Format that reads the template "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}" and figures out where the holes are. That work was happening on every single call, and my template never changed.

The template gets reparsed every time

When you call string.Format(format, args), the runtime has to walk that format string, find the {0}, {1:...}, {2:...} placeholders, pull out the alignment and the format specifiers, and only then start stitching the output together. That parsing step is pure overhead if the template is a constant, which it almost always is. You wrote the template once in your source code. The runtime rediscovers its structure five million times.

CompositeFormat is the fix, and it's about as simple as it gets. You parse the template once into a CompositeFormat object, then hand that object to string.Format instead of the raw string. The holes are already located. The call just fills them.

const string Template = "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}";

// Parsed once, up front.
var parsed = CompositeFormat.Parse(Template);

// Later, in the hot loop:
string a = string.Format(ci, Template, id, when, amount);   // reparses Template
string b = string.Format(ci, parsed,   id, when, amount);   // reuses the parse

So I counted. I formatted the same CSV line five million times through each path, best of five rounds, summing the line lengths so the compiler couldn't throw the work away, and tracking allocations with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread.

const int Iterations = 5_000_000;
var when = new DateTime(2026, 11, 7, 8, 11, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc);
const decimal amount = 1234.56m;
var ci = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;

var parsed = CompositeFormat.Parse("{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}");

long sinkA = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
    sinkA += string.Format(ci, "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}", i, when, amount).Length;

long sinkB = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
    sinkB += string.Format(ci, parsed, i, when, amount).Length;

Here's what came back:

Runtime: .NET 10.0.14
5,000,000 formats, best of 5

  string.Format(string)            837.9 ms    167.6 ns/call    838.5 MB
  string.Format(CompositeFormat)   517.7 ms    103.5 ns/call    457.0 MB

The time ratio bounced between about 1.4x and 1.6x depending on the round, which is honest for a microbenchmark running in a container I don't fully control. I care about the ratio, not the absolute milliseconds. But the allocation number didn't bounce at all: string.Format(string) churned 838.5 MB, the CompositeFormat path 457.0 MB. That's a steady 381 MB of garbage I was handing the GC for no reason other than relocating the same three braces over and over. Both paths produced byte-identical output, which is the whole point. Same answer, less work.

The allocation gap is the part worth sitting with. The reparsing doesn't just cost CPU; it allocates on the way through, and that allocation is what eventually turns into GC pauses in a service that's doing this constantly. Cutting it nearly in half for a one-line change is a good trade.

When this is a waste of time

Here's the caveat, and it's a real one: CompositeFormat only pays off when you reuse the same template a lot. If you're formatting a string once, or a handful of times, parsing it into a CompositeFormat first is strictly more work than just calling string.Format with the literal. You've added an allocation and a line of code to save nothing. This is a hot-path tool. A log line formatted per-request, a CSV row per record, a template rendered in a tight loop — those are where it earns its keep. The welcome email you send once? Leave it alone.

My honest opinion: for most code, interpolated strings ($"{id},{when:yyyy-MM-dd}") are already the right default, and the compiler handles them well. CompositeFormat isn't competing with those. It's for the specific case where your template lives in a variable or a resource file, gets reused heavily, and you were reaching for string.Format anyway. In that narrow spot it's close to free to adopt. The one gotcha: CompositeFormat.Parse validates the template up front, so a malformed template throws at parse time instead of at the first format call. I'd call that a feature.

The thing I like about it is how little it asks. You're not rewriting the formatting, not switching APIs, not learning a new builder. You pull the parse out of the loop. One line moves up, and a few hundred megabytes of garbage stop existing. That's the kind of change I'll take every time.

Have you found a spot in your own code where the template was constant but you were paying to rediscover it? I'd like to hear where it bit you.

— still benchmarking the things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: How I audit AI-written code — and the bug that proved why
articles.description: I ship as an AI-augmented solo builder, but I never trust what the model produces. Here's the review discipline that caught a missing Android permission in every earlier release build.
articles.body_html:
I build most of my software as an AI-augmented solo developer. I write the spec, I own the architecture, and I drive Claude Code and Cursor through the implementation. But there is one rule I never break: I audit what actually ships, not what the model tells me it produced.

Here is the bug that turned that rule into a habit.

The symptom that shouldn't exist

CoalTrack is an attendance and payroll app for coal-mining crews. During closed testing, a handful of devices simply could not reach the server — no error, no retry loop that recovered, just silence. The code looked correct. The API was up. Every earlier build had "worked on my machine."

So I stopped reading the source and started reading the artifact. I pulled apart the signed app bundle and inspected the merged AndroidManifest.xml that Google Play actually receives.

The android.permission.INTERNET line wasn't there.

Why the source lied

In a multi-module Flutter build, the manifest you write is not the manifest that ships. Plugins, build types and manifest merging all rewrite it. A change somewhere upstream had dropped the INTERNET permission from the merged result — so on a fresh install with no cached grant, the app had no network at all. On my phone it worked because the permission had been granted by an earlier build and survived the upgrade.

Reading the source would never have found this. Reading the shipped bundle found it in minutes.

The discipline

That is the whole point of AI-augmented work done responsibly. The model accelerates the typing; it does not absolve me of verification. Concretely, that means:

  • Verify the artifact, not the intent. Inspect the built bundle, the merged manifest, the generated SQL migration — the thing that actually runs.
  • Write the risky logic twice, on purpose. CoalTrack computes Indonesian statutory payroll in a PHP service and a Dart mirror, then cross-checks them with mirrored tests. If the model drifts on one side, the other catches it.
  • Gate everything with tests. 400+ automated tests run in CI before any signed build. AI writing more code is only safe if more code is also checked.
  • Read the diff like a reviewer, not an author. The model is an eager junior engineer. Treat its output that way.

The takeaway

"AI wrote it" is not a defect and it is not a badge. The engineering is still mine — the spec, the review, the decision about what is correct. The productivity is real, but so is the responsibility. Ship the audit, not the optimism.

From a 2:00 AM PagerDuty Nightmare to a 13-Second Automated Hotfix with Zero-Trust Human Governance.

By Lokesh Sai — Built with Switch AI & WeMakeDevs

📺 Project Links & Live Proof

  • Live Video Demonstration: Watch Live Walkthrough on Google Drive
  • GitHub Submission Workspace: lokebuilds/praesync-workspace
  • Target Microservice Repo: lokebuilds/praesync-core
  • Live Verified Pull Requests: PR #4 · PR #5 · PR #9

⚡ 1. The 2:00 AM Reality: The Midnight Sev-1 Crisis

Every engineer who has ever carried an on-call pager knows this feeling:

It’s 2:14 AM. Your phone violently buzzes on the nightstand.

[CRITICAL SEV-1] auth-db-primary connection pool exhausted. 504 Gateway Timeouts across Checkout & Auth APIs.

Your heart rate spikes. You stumble out of bed, open your laptop in a dark room, and join an emergency Slack war room. For the next 45 minutes, three senior engineers are frantically juggling context:

  1. Engineer A is running grep and awk across thousands of lines of Datadog socket logs.
  2. Engineer B is trying to remember which commit introduced the unclosed database cursor.
  3. Engineer C is cloning the repository locally, attempting to reproduce the connection timeout, and frantically drafting an emergency hotpatch.

According to the PagerDuty State of Digital Operations Report, the average Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) for enterprise P1/Sev-1 incidents ranges between 35 and 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, Gartner calculates that enterprise IT downtime averages $5,600 per minute. That single 45-minute midnight panic costs the business over $250,000 in direct revenue loss, SLA penalties, and engineering burnout.

Over 70% of that MTTR is completely wasted on manual triaging, coordinating between fragmented tools, and navigating human fatigue.

I asked myself a simple question:

What if our AI coding agents didn't live trapped inside isolated terminal windows, but operated as collaborative, communicative SRE teammates directly inside our team’s Slack war room?

That is why I built Praesync.

🧠 2. The Core Idea: Turning Solo Agents into Team SREs via Switch AI

Modern AI tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex are exceptional at generating code in an isolated terminal. But production incidents don’t happen in isolation. They happen inside team chat channels (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord) where people and systems must collaborate under high stakes.

Switch AI was the missing link.

Switch transforms ordinary chat channels into stateful multi-agent rooms. Instead of a single monolithic prompt trying to do everything (and inevitably hallucinating or suffering from prompt bleed), Switch allows you to define specialized agent roles with distinct instructions, capabilities, and handoff protocols.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              PRAESYNC MULTI-AGENT TOPOLOGY                             │
│                                                                                        │
│   Datadog Alert ──► Slack (#incidents) <─── Switch Bridge ───> Switch Room Memory      │
│                                                                      │                 │
│         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┐   │
│         ▼                                    ▼                                     ▼   │
│   @swarm-investigator                  @swarm-patcher                         @swarm-ops │
│   (Telemetry Parser)                  (GitHub ReAct Patcher)              (Human Gatekeeper) │
│         │                                    │                                     │   │
│         └────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                              ▼                                         │
│                      Switch Agent Protocol (SSE In, HTTP Out)                          │
│                                              ▼                                         │
│                      Praesync Tool Sidecar Engine (main.py)                            │
│                      POST /v1/chat/completions & PyGithub API                          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In Praesync, Switch coordinates three distinct teammates inside our Slack war room:

  1. @swarm-investigator (Root Cause Isolation): Parses distributed stack traces, isolates failing microservices, and bounds the incident scope.
  2. @swarm-patcher (Autonomous Systems Programmer): Queries the live GitHub API, inspects the deployed production code, synthesizes an atomic Python hotpatch, and commits a live Pull Request.
  3. @swarm-ops (Human Gatekeeper): Enforces enterprise zero-trust compliance. No code reaches production without human authorization.

🛠️ 3. How We Configured Switch AI: The Declarative Blueprint

Setting up Switch was refreshingly clean. Everything is declared in a single, version-controlled YAML template (praesync.template.yaml):

agents:
  - name: "{team}-investigator"
    description: "Analyzes stack traces and identifies root causes"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    machine: "{machine}"
    instructions: |
      You are a senior Site Reliability Engineer. Read the provided error log,
      identify the failing microservice, and state the root cause in exactly two sentences.

  - name: "{team}-patcher"
    description: "Writes Python hotfixes and generates PR diffs"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    machine: "{machine}"
    instructions: |
      You are the core maintainer. Inspect live microservice source code, write the
      Python fix for the bug identified by Investigator, and call create_github_pr.

  - name: "{team}-ops"
    description: "Handles deployment and PR merges"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    machine: "{machine}"
    instructions: |
      You are the deployment gatekeeper. Wait for the Human Lead to type "Approve and Deploy".
      Acknowledge the command and confirm canary rollout initiation.

room:
  name: "{team}-war-room"
  description: "Sev-1 Incident Command and Hotpatch execution room"
  bridge: "{bridge}"
  agents: ["{team}-investigator", "{team}-patcher", "{team}-ops"]
  users: ["*"]

kickoff: |
  @{team}-investigator, @{team}-patcher, and @{team}-ops: Praesync Incident Command online. Awaiting Sev-1 telemetry.

The Switch Agent Protocol in Action

  • Server-Sent Events (SSE In): Switch streams real-time messages from the Slack channel into the agents' unified room log.
  • HTTP Out (/v1/chat/completions): Agents communicate with our backend tool sidecar (main.py) over standard OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
  • Daemon Webhook (/webhook/switch): Switch informs main.py of user approvals and room handoffs, which instantly stream to our Next.js HUD via WebSockets.

🔬 4. The Deep-Dive: How Praesync Writes Real GitHub PRs in 13 Seconds

Many AI demo prototypes simply output markdown code snippets to a chat window and stop. In a production enterprise, that is useless.

Praesync performs a true Read → Analyze → Patch → Commit cycle against a live microservice repository (lokebuilds/praesync-core):

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor DD as Datadog Webhook
    participant SW as Switch War Room (Slack)
    participant INV as @swarm-investigator
    participant PAT as @swarm-patcher
    participant GH as GitHub API (PyGithub)
    participant HUD as Praesync HUD (Next.js)
    actor SRE as Human SRE Lead
    participant OPS as @swarm-ops

    DD->>SW: Sev-1 DB Connection Pool Exhaustion Alert
    SW->>INV: Alert Ingested
    INV->>HUD: Broadcast Alert & Start Stopwatch (ws://)
    INV->>PAT: Handoff Isolated Root Cause & Scope
    PAT->>GH: repo.get_contents("app/database/connection.py")
    GH-->>PAT: Return Live Source (1,661 bytes)
    PAT->>PAT: Gemini 3.5 Flash ReAct Reasoning & Patch Generation
    PAT->>GH: create_git_ref(branch) + update_file() + create_pull()
    GH-->>PAT: Live PR URL (https://github.com/lokebuilds/praesync-core/pull/9)
    PAT->>HUD: Stop MTTR Clock (13.2s) & Render In-HUD Code Diff
    PAT->>SW: Post PR Resolution Card to Slack
    Note over HUD,SRE: Gatekeeper State: AWAITING_APPROVAL
    SRE->>HUD: Click [APPROVE & DEPLOY →]
    HUD->>OPS: POST /api/deploy/approve
    OPS->>HUD: State Transition: ROLLOUT_ACTIVE (3 Zones)
    OPS->>SW: :rocket: [HUMAN SIGNOFF VERIFIED — CANARY ACTIVE]

Step 1: The Live Repository Read

@swarm-patcher does not hallucinate code out of thin air. It uses PyGithub to fetch the exact file currently deployed on main:

# Authenticate with GitHub PAT and fetch live production source
auth = Auth.Token(github_pat)
gh = Github(auth=auth)
repo = gh.get_repo("lokebuilds/praesync-core")

remote_file = repo.get_contents("app/database/connection.py", ref="main")
live_repo_code = remote_file.decoded_content.decode("utf-8")

Step 2: Context Injection & Gemini 3.5 Flash ReAct Reasoning

We inject the raw stack trace and the real 1,661 bytes of production Python code into Google’s blazing-fast Gemini-3.5-Flash model. In our benchmarks across 50 Google AI Studio models, gemini-3.5-flash clocked in at 1.93 seconds with native tool calling:

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are swarm-patcher. Inspect the live code and call create_github_pr."},
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Alert: {alert}\n\n=== CURRENT LIVE REPO CODE ===\n{live_repo_code}"}
]

Step 3: Atomic GitHub Commit & Pull Request Creation

When the agent invokes the create_github_pr tool, PyGithub executes native git operations:

  1. Grabs the latest commit SHA of main.
  2. Creates an ephemeral branch: hotfix/sev1-<timestamp>.
  3. Commits the patched file with an audit trail message.
  4. Opens the official Pull Request against main.

Here is an actual real-world diff generated by Praesync on lokebuilds/praesync-core/pull/9:

- def get_db_connection(dsn: str = None):
-     # Unbounded connection with zero retry backoff
-     return psycopg2.connect(dsn)

+ MAX_RETRIES = int(os.getenv("DB_MAX_RETRIES", "5"))
+ INITIAL_BACKOFF = float(os.getenv("DB_INITIAL_BACKOFF", "1.0"))
+ BACKOFF_FACTOR = float(os.getenv("DB_BACKOFF_FACTOR", "2.0"))
+ CONNECT_TIMEOUT = int(os.getenv("DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT", "10"))
+
+ def get_db_connection(dsn: str = None):
+     """Establishes connection with exponential backoff & timeout guards."""
+     backoff = INITIAL_BACKOFF
+     for attempt in range(1, MAX_RETRIES + 1):
+         try:
+             return psycopg2.connect(dsn, connect_timeout=CONNECT_TIMEOUT)
+         except (OperationalError, Exception) as exc:
+             if attempt == MAX_RETRIES: raise exc
+             time.sleep(backoff)
+             backoff *= BACKOFF_FACTOR

🛡️ 5. Zero-Trust Safety: The Human Gatekeeper Protocol

The #1 fear engineering leaders have with AI agents is loss of control. What if an agent hallucinates a destructive patch or gets triggered by a false alarm?

In Praesync, zero autonomous code can ever reach production without human verification:

  1. In-HUD Diff Inspector Modal: When the PR is generated, the on-call engineer can click ⚡ PREVIEW HOTPATCH DIFF right inside the Linear-style HUD. A dark syntax-highlighted modal displays the unified diff without forcing the engineer to switch browser tabs.
  2. The @swarm-ops Gatekeeper: The deployment pipeline enters an explicit AWAITING_APPROVAL state. The SRE verifies the diff and clicks APPROVE & DEPLOY → (or types "Approve and Deploy" in Slack).
  3. Canary Rollout Active: Stage 3 transitions to glowing emerald, and @swarm-ops broadcasts the verified sign-off card to the Slack war room: :rocket: [HUMAN SIGNOFF VERIFIED — CANARY ROLLOUT ACTIVE across zones us-east-1a, us-east-1b]. Sev-1 incident closed.

Edge-Case Handling & Fault Tolerance

If malformed telemetry or unexpected inputs are received:

  • The system’s Adaptive Safe-Shield ensures it never throws a 500 error or crashes.
  • And even if a bogus PR is created, the Human Gatekeeper stops it dead in its tracks. The SRE inspects the diff, recognizes the spam, and closes the PR without approving.

📊 6. The Hard Numbers: Empirical Benchmark Results

Every metric below was benchmarked live on our production cluster test runs:

Operational Metric Traditional SRE On-Call Praesync + Switch AI Swarm Measured Impact
Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) 35 – 45 Minutes 12.8 – 14.2 Seconds 99.4% Reduction
Root Cause Isolation 15–20 mins (distributed trace grep) 1.8 Seconds (@swarm-investigator) Instant telemetry parsing
Patch & Pull Request Creation 15–25 mins (manual branching & PR) 11.2 Seconds (@swarm-patcher via PyGithub) 100% Autonomous git commits
Human Governance High-pressure, sleep-deprived reviews 1-Click in-HUD Diff Review & Sign-Off Zero context-switching
Risk of Unverified Deploys High (rushed manual hotfixes) Zero (Strict Human Gatekeeper required) Fully audited compliance
Operational Inference Cost $150+/hr in SRE salary overhead ~$0.002 per incident (Gemini 3.5 Flash) Minimal infrastructure cost

💡 7. What I Learned Building with Switch AI (Tips for First-Time Users)

Building with Switch AI was an eye-opening architectural journey. Here are my key engineering takeaways:

1. Declarative Room Topologies Prevent Prompt Bleed

If you try to give a single agent instructions to "investigate the bug, then write the code, then deploy it, but ask for permission first", the LLM frequently jumps ahead or forgets instructions. By splitting the workflow into investigator → patcher → ops across a Switch room, each agent has a laser-focused context boundary.

2. Standard OpenAI-Compatible Endpoints Make Tooling Trivial

Switch’s protocol uses standard HTTP completions out. This meant I could write my tool execution engine in standard FastAPI (main.py), attach native Python libraries like PyGithub, and expose it seamlessly to Switch without proprietary SDK lock-in.

3. What I’d Love to See in Switch Next

  • Native Slack Block Kit Action Buttons: Allowing human leads to click interactive [Approve] and [Rollback] buttons directly inside Slack message cards.
  • Built-in Local Tunneling: Having an integrated daemon tunnel (like a built-in Cloudflare Tunnel) would make local development with cloud chat providers zero-config on Windows.

🎯 8. Conclusion: The Future of Incident Command

The future of SRE is not replacing engineers with black-box AI. It is giving human engineers autonomous, communicative teammates that handle the cognitive heavy lifting during high-stress outages.

By combining Switch AI’s collaborative room topology, Google Gemini-3.5-Flash’s high-speed reasoning, and PyGithub’s native execution, Praesync proves that a 45-minute midnight Sev-1 outage can be safely investigated, patched, reviewed, and deployed in under 15 seconds.

What I Built

A couple of weeks ago I recorded a three-minute product pitch and watched the playback with the sound muted. By the forty-second mark my shoulders had crept up toward my ears, my jaw had locked, and I was reading off my screen scroller at 190 words per minute without taking a single abdominal breath. Every teleprompter on the market is a dumb motorized conveyor belt: it scrolls at a fixed pixel velocity whether you are calm and grounded or rushing through your best lines out of stage fright.

I built StagePulse, a consent-first bio-adaptive teleprompter, vocal presence studio, and reactive auditorium built on @smartspectra/node-sdk v3.4.0.

Instead of treating physiological sensing as a passive chart on a dashboard, StagePulse wires your live optical and physiological signals directly into the mechanics of rehearsal and stagecraft:

How It Responds to Human Signals

StagePulse integrates all four SmartSpectra metric bundles (faceMetrics, cardioMetrics, breathingMetrics, edaMetrics), all 16 ValidationCode states, and sdk.requestInsight() across a 5-Act Progressive Warm-Up Timeline that respects Presage's real measurement latency and confidence gates:

  1. Act I (0s Immediate Optical & Biomechanical Lock):
    • Reads .at(-1) on every repeated protobuf array emitted by decodeMetrics(buf).

  5. Act V (60s Autonomic HRV & Stage Presence Matrix, confidence >= 50):

Consent and Data Handling

Physiological and facial telemetry deserves strict boundaries. StagePulse enforces five concrete safeguards in code:

  1. Mandatory Pre-Hardware Consent Gate: StagePulseEngine.startSession() (src/spectra-engine.mjs) throws CONSENT_REQUIRED if consentConfirmed !== true. Neither camera capture nor file streaming starts before the speaker explicitly confirms consent in the Greenroom modal.

  3. Privacy Wireframe Cloak (Default ON): Raw videoOutput RGB frames are suppressed by default. Instead, computeFaceGeometry() normalizes 52 anatomical landmark coordinates (0.0..1.0) and renders a geometric wireframe mesh on #wireframe-canvas. Zero camera frames are ever written to disk.
  4. Volatile 32 KB Ring Buffer & One-Click CSPRNG Wipe: Session scalars are held in a fixed 4,096-element Float64Array (32,768 bytes) in Node.js process RAM. Triggering POST /api/privacy/wipe stops and destroys the native SDK session, overwrites all 32,768 bytes with cryptographic random noise via crypto.randomFillSync(), computes a verifiable SHA-256 digest receipt, and zeroes every array.
  5. Strictly Non-Medical Ergonomic Framing: All feedback is framed and designed strictly as stagecraft, vocal pacing, and presentation ergonomics coaching, never as medical diagnosis, clinical monitoring, or treatment.

Why your crypto checkout only needs one wallet address

I run a small store that sells digital goods. For two weeks it accepted exactly one thing: BEP20 USDT on BSC. Technically the payment flow worked — the RPC was healthy, the watcher was armed, orders were quoted correctly.

Zero sales. Twenty-three inquiries, four of them reached the payment page, and all four left at exactly the same step: the moment they saw the payment screen.

It took me an embarrassing amount of time to understand why. The buyers had money. They just didn't have money on that chain. One had USDC on Base. Another had USDT on Ethereum. A third had something on Polygon. Every single one of them would have paid instantly if the checkout had said "USDC on Base" instead of "USDT on BSC".

So I rebuilt the rail. One wallet address, six chains, two stablecoins, eleven ways to pay. This post is what I learned doing it, including the four things that cost me real debugging time.

The insight that makes it simple

The obvious approach is wrong. If you support six chains, you might think you need six sets of order numbers — one per chain — so you can tell which payment belongs to which order.

You don't. The amount is the identity. The chain is just transport.

When an invoice is created, give it a unique micro-amount. Not 19.00 — 19.13. The buyer is asked for exactly 19.13 in USDT or USDC, on whichever chain they like. Your watcher scans every enabled chain for Transfer events addressed to your wallet, and matches on the amount.

Two orders can never share an amount, so there's no ambiguity. The buyer never has to tell you which chain they used. And adding a seventh chain requires zero changes to the order model — you just watch one more chain.

The one thing you must get right: uniqueness has to be enforced globally across all pending invoices, and it has to be enforced before you issue the invoice, not after.

What the transfer event actually looks like

ERC-20 and BEP-20 share the same event signature:

topics[0] = 0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef
topics[1] = the buyer
topics[2] = you (padded to 32 bytes)
data      = amount, in the token's base units

Filtering by topics[2] is not an optimization. It is the difference between a working watcher and one that melts your RPC provider.

On BSC, a 200-block window carries roughly 7,600 Transfer events across all of USDT. If you pull every transfer and filter client-side, you download all 7,600 to find the zero that are yours. Filter server-side and you get an empty array in 200ms.

const TRANSFER = '0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef';
const pad = a => '0x' + a.toLowerCase().replace(/^0x/, '').padStart(64, '0');

const logs = await rpc('eth_getLogs', [{
  address: tokenContract,
  fromBlock: '0x' + from.toString(16),
  toBlock:   '0x' + to.toString(16),
  topics: [TRANSFER, null, pad(myWallet)],   // <- null means "any sender"
}]);

Trap 1: decimals is not the same across chains for the same symbol

This is the one that silently ruins you.

  • BSC's BSC-USD (which everyone calls USDT) uses 18 decimals.
  • Ethereum's USDT uses 6 decimals.
  • So does Polygon's, Arbitrum's, Optimism's, and Base's USDC.

Hardcode 18 and every non-BSC payment is off by a factor of 10¹². Hardcode 6 and BSC is off in the other direction. Either way the order never matches, the buyer has paid, and nothing happens. That's the worst possible failure: silent, on the money path, and invisible until someone complains.

Read it from the contract once and cache it:

// decimals() is selector 0x313ce567
const raw = await rpc('eth_call', [{ to: tokenContract, data: '0x313ce567' }, 'latest']);
const decimals = parseInt(raw, 16);

Trap 2: never use floating point for amounts

19.88 * 1e6 happens to equal 19880000 in JavaScript. It's not guaranteed to for every amount — and when it isn't, you lose one base unit, the transfer no longer matches your quote exactly, and the order hangs forever while the money sits in your wallet.

Do the arithmetic on strings with BigInt:

function amountToUnits(text, decimals) {
  const [i, f = ''] = String(text).split('.');
  return BigInt(i) * (10n ** BigInt(decimals))
       + BigInt((f + '0'.repeat(decimals)).slice(0, decimals));
}

function unitsToAmount(raw, decimals) {
  const s = BigInt(raw).toString().padStart(decimals + 1, '0');
  const cut = s.length - decimals;
  return `${s.slice(0, cut)}.${s.slice(cut, cut + 2).padEnd(2, '0')}`;
}

Round-trip both directions in a test. 0.07, 19.10, 139.99 — these are the ones that catch you.

Trap 3: two RPC providers lie about eth_getLogs

Measured from one machine, November 2025:

chain blocks per eth_getLogs round trip note
BSC 1000 375 ms 18 decimals
Ethereum 10000 578 ms 6 decimals
Base 3000 369 ms USDC only
Polygon 5000 ~540 ms 6 decimals
Optimism 5000 ~522 ms 6 decimals
Arbitrum 3000 ~530 ms see below

Two things that are not in anyone's documentation:

arbitrum-one-rpc.publicnode.com returns HTTP 403 for eth_getLogs. It answers eth_blockNumber perfectly, so your health check goes green. You have to use https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc.

1rpc.io does not implement eth_getLogs at all. It returns -32000 The method eth_getLogs is not supported. Same problem: everything else works, so it looks healthy right up until the moment you need logs.

Both cost me an hour each because the failure is invisible to a naive health check. Test eth_getLogs specifically, not just connectivity.

Trap 4: a failed range must never advance the cursor

The cursor is your only defence against losing a payment. If a block range fails, lastBlock must stay exactly where it was, and the next tick retries the same range.

while (from <= head) {
  const to = Math.min(from + blockStep - 1, head);
  try {
    const logs = await rpc('eth_getLogs', [{ /* from..to */ }]);
    for (const lg of logs) applyPayment(/* ... */);
  } catch (e) {
    state.lastError = e.message;
    break;              // do NOT advance
  }
  state.lastBlock = to; // only on success
  from = to + 1;
}

Slow is fine. Skipping blocks is not.

And the mirror image: if your process was down for six hours, do not replay six hours of history. Jump to head - blockStep * 20. Replaying risks matching somebody else's old transfer to a fresh invoice.

Two more things that will bite you

Exchange withdrawals deduct a fee. A buyer who sends 19.27 from Binance can land 18.27 on chain. If you only match exactly, that sale is lost and the buyer is out of pocket with nothing to show. Accept a shortfall up to ~8% (or a fixed 1.5 USDT, whichever is larger), pick the closest pending invoice, and record the order as underpaid.

Only 98 cent-values exist per price point. This one I found through a test, not through design. If your quote is price + random(1..98) cents, then at 19 USDT you have exactly 98 distinct amounts. The 99th concurrent invoice collides with an existing one, and now two buyers are racing for one transfer — the first one wins, the second pays and gets nothing. Tier the pool (+0.01..+0.98, then +1.00..+4.99, then +5.00..+9.99) and refuse to issue an invoice when it's exhausted. Refusing is much better than issuing a doomed one.

How to verify it works without spending money

Write a fake RPC. Return a Transfer log shaped exactly like the real thing — right topic order, right padding, right data width — and assert that your order flips to paid, that the recorded chain is the one the money "arrived" on, and that a mismatched amount does not deliver.

Then assert the nasty cases:

  • Two sellers, same amount, one receives — the other must stay pending.
  • A transfer to a third-party address with the right amount — must be ignored.
  • RPC throws — the cursor must not move.
  • 200 concurrent invoices — zero duplicate amounts.

That suite runs in under a second and catches every bug I've described above.

The takeaway

Supporting six chains sounds like six times the work. It isn't. It's the same watcher pointed at six RPC endpoints, plus one rule: the amount identifies the order, the chain is only how the money got there.

The hard part was never the crypto. It was the four traps — decimals, floating point, lying RPCs, and cursor discipline — every one of which fails silently on the money path.

I packaged the working implementation, the measured numbers, and the test suite as a kit if you'd rather not rediscover all of this: PayLink Kit. There's also a live instance you can poke at without buying anything — paste any EVM address and it'll generate a real payment link: https://csvtriage.com/paylink/

Either way, the four traps above are yours now. That's the part that actually costs the time.

Why Background Location Tracking Fails in React Native (And How I Fixed It with JSI & TurboModules)

About the Author

Hi, I’m Punith Manthri, a Senior React Native Developer with 5 years of experience specializing in native module bridging, JSI, and the New Architecture. I am the creator and maintainer of react-native-pdf-jsi, a high-performance PDF library built on JSI that has surpassed 350,000+ downloads on npm (with over 65,000 weekly downloads). I spend most of my time writing native Kotlin, Swift, and C++ to push the boundaries of what React Native can do.

If you have ever built a React Native app that requires background location (like a delivery, fitness, or fleet-tracking app), you know the nightmare.

You write the code, test it in the simulator, and it works perfectly. You put the phone in your pocket, walk around the block, and look at your database. Half the data is missing.

I’ve used the major players (expo-location, Transistorsoft) and they are great, but I kept hitting the same production walls. So, I decided to build a native-only solution from scratch.

Here is what I learned about why background location breaks in React Native, and how the New Architecture (JSI/TurboModules) finally solves it.

1. JS Background Tasks are a Trap

If you rely on expo-task-manager or standard JS background tasks, your location logic runs in the JavaScript thread.

The Problem:
Modern mobile OSes (especially Android) are ruthless. When the device runs low on RAM, or sits idle for too long, the OS will kill your app process to save battery. When the process dies, the JS runtime dies. Your background task stops, and you only find out days later when your data has massive gaps.

The Fix:
The tracking engine must be 100% native.

  • On Android, this means a Kotlin Foreground Service using FusedLocationProvider.
  • On iOS, this means Swift CLLocationManager with background modes enabled.

The JS thread should only be used to update the UI. The actual tracking and network requests must be detached from React entirely.

2. Motion Detection Needs to "Fail Open"

To save battery, most libraries use motion sensors (accelerometer, significant motion) to "park" the GPS when the device is stationary.

The Problem:
Android vendor ROMs (like Xiaomi or Samsung) and iOS CMMotionActivityManager frequently misclassify "slow movement" (like a hiker or a phone in a bag) as "stationary." The GPS silently sleeps, and you lose the route.

The Fix:
The motion gate must fail open. If the OS denies motion permissions, or the sensor fails to trigger, the engine must default to always-on GPS. It should never pause silently without a clear error state.

3. The "Duplicate Upload" Nightmare

If a user goes through a tunnel or a basement, they lose network. If you handle your retry logic in JavaScript, and the app is killed mid-request, you either lose the location points or duplicate them on your backend when the app restarts.

The Fix:
You need a native SQLite queue (using Room on Android).

  1. Every location fix is written to SQLite before anything else.
  2. Uploads are batched with Idempotency Keys.
  3. If a 5xx error or timeout occurs, the native layer uses exponential backoff with jitter.

By keeping the queue native, the sync survives process death. When the app reboots, the native layer picks up exactly where it left off.

4. The Apple & Google Store Rejection Problem

Background location is the #1 reason apps get rejected from the App Store and Google Play. Apple's "Prominent Disclosure" requirements and Google's "Foreground Service" declarations are a compliance nightmare.

The Fix:
You need precise Info.plist purpose strings, clear AndroidManifest.xml foreground service types, and a privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy).

How the New Architecture (JSI) Changes the Game

Older background location libraries relied on the legacy bridge, which meant high latency and serialization overhead when sending high-frequency location points to JS.

By building exclusively for the New Architecture, I was able to use:

  • TurboModules: To ensure synchronous, instant initialization of the native tracking service.
  • JSI (JavaScript Interface): To query the native SQLite queue state directly from the JS thread without blocking or asynchronous overhead.

What I Built

Because I couldn't find an open-source solution that handled all of the above natively, I built React Native Background Location Pro.

It is a complete, production-grade SDK that runs Kotlin and Swift behind a TurboModule (JSI). It includes:

  • 🛡️ Self-healing tracking (survives app kills, reboots, and OS updates).
  • 📶 Offline-first native SQLite queues.
  • 🏪 A "Store Approval Blueprint" to help you pass Apple/Google review.
  • 🗺️ A live map dashboard for testing.

Try it for free

I know commercial SDKs can be a hard sell, so I published a free debug evaluation build on npm. It runs the full production native engine (Kotlin/Swift binaries) with zero time limits in debug mode. You can test crash recovery, airplane mode, and the native queues in your own app before deciding if it's right for you.

View the source & docs:

👉 NPM Package

Install the free eval:


bash
npm i react-native-background-location-pro-eval

articles.title: I Intercepted Network Traffic From 10 Popular Online JWT Decoders. 4 Of Them Secretly Uploaded My Bearer Tokens to Remote Servers.
articles.description: We captured HTTP network traffic across 10 popular web-based JWT decoders. 4 of them transmitted full Bearer tokens over the wire. Here is what we found and how we built an offline in-browser JWKS signature verifier with WebCrypto.
articles.body_html:
It happened during a late-night staging outage at 2:14 AM.

Our microservices were rejecting inter-service authentication requests with mysterious 401 Unauthorized responses. The OAuth2 Bearer token in my terminal was a massive 1,400-character string encoded in Base64URL.

Like thousands of software engineers every single day, I almost did what has become muscle memory: copy the token, open a browser tab, and paste it into the first online JWT decoder that pops up on Google.

Then I paused.

That token was minted for our billing service. Its decrypted payload contained internal customer UUIDs, tenant identifiers, elevated OAuth authorization scopes, and an active lifetime of 24 hours.

If that online tool sent my token across the internet, our production secrets and user claims would be floating in third-party Nginx access logs, reverse proxy caches, and analytics databases.

So instead of pasting it, I opened Wireshark, fired up Chrome DevTools with network inspection enabled, and decided to run a structured empirical test:

What actually happens behind the scenes when you paste an authentication token into the web's most popular JWT decoders?

Here is what our network captures revealed, the silent signature vulnerability we uncovered across 200 tampered tokens, and how we engineered a 100% client-side, zero-telemetry in-browser JWKS verification engine using the native W3C Web Cryptography API.

The Network Interception Experiment: 10 Tools, 1 Proxy, 0 Excuses

We collected 10 popular web-based JWT decoders and formatters frequently recommended across Google Search and developer forums.

Using an isolated Chromium instance routing all outbound TCP/HTTP traffic through an intercepting proxy, we pasted identical test tokens into each tool and recorded every network call triggered upon typing or pasting.

The Results:

  • 6 Tools (60%) executed entirely in JavaScript using local string manipulation (atob() or custom Base64 decoding).
  • 4 Tools (40%) fired outbound HTTP POST requests transmitting the full Bearer token to remote backend endpoints.

Some of these remote calls were labeled /api/decode or /v1/parse. Others were telemetry payloads sent to third-party product analytics services that captured the entire input field contents as an event attribute.

Why This Is an Enterprise Security Nightmare:

  1. Bearer Token Replay: A Bearer token is a bearer credential. Anyone who possesses it can impersonate the subject until the exp (expiration) timestamp lapses.
  2. PII and Data Sovereignty Violations: Enterprise JWTs frequently contain user emails, IP metadata, and organizational roles. Transmitting these claims to unknown cloud servers violates GDPR, HIPAA, and SOC 2 data protection boundaries.
  3. Telemetry & Log Retention: Even if a cloud tool claims "we do not store your data", standard cloud infrastructure (Cloudflare, AWS ALB, Datadog, ELK stacks) routinely logs incoming request headers and bodies unless explicitly scrubbed.

The Silent Failure: Testing 200 Tampered Tokens with the alg: none Exploit

Exfiltrating tokens is bad enough. But we discovered an even more dangerous flaw: almost every online decoder lies to you about whether a token is actually valid.

A JSON Web Token consists of three distinct parts separated by dots:

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

Most online decoders simply split the string by . and call Base64URL decode on the first two segments. Because the payload renders as clean JSON, the user interface proudly displays a green checkmark or a badge saying: Valid JWT Token.

It is not valid. It is merely parseable.

To demonstrate this hazard, we generated 200 cryptographically signed RS256 tokens and systematically tampered with them:

  1. We modified the payload claim from "role": "viewer" to "role": "admin".
  2. In half the tokens, we changed the header algorithm to "alg": "none".
  3. In the other half, we left "alg": "RS256" but replaced the signature with random bytes.

When we fed these 200 forged tokens into traditional online decoders:

  • 78% of tools rendered the forged "admin" payload without any visual warning whatsoever.
  • 38% explicitly displayed green "Valid" badges simply because the JSON syntax was structurally well-formed!

If an engineer uses these tools to inspect why a backend service is rejecting an incoming request, the tool misleads them into believing the token is legitimate when the signature is mathematically invalid.

The Asymmetric Breakthrough: Why JWKS Can Be Safely Verified Client-Side

Many developers assume signature verification must happen on a secure backend server.

For symmetric algorithms like HS256 (HMAC-SHA256), that is correct: HMAC uses a shared secret password. If you expose your HMAC secret to the browser, anyone can mint arbitrary authentication tokens and compromise your entire system.

However, modern enterprise authentication architectures (Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, Keycloak, Firebase, Google Cloud Identity) do not use symmetric keys. They use Asymmetric Cryptography: RS256 (RSA-SHA256) or ES256 (ECDSA P-256).

How Asymmetric Auth Works:

  • Private Key: Stays strictly locked inside the Identity Provider's hardware security module (HSM). It is used exclusively to sign tokens.
  • Public Key: Published openly to the world at a standard discovery endpoint: 
  https://your-auth-domain.com/.well-known/jwks.json

Because the Public Key is non-confidential, your browser can safely download the JWKS document and mathematically verify the token's digital signature right inside local memory.

No secrets are exposed. No bearer tokens leave the client.

The Implementation: Verifying RS256 & ES256 Tokens with W3C WebCrypto

Modern browsers ship with the W3C Web Cryptography API (window.crypto.subtle). This is not a slow third-party JavaScript library; it is a compiled, hardware-accelerated cryptographic engine built directly into Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.

Here is the exact 4-step pipeline to verify asymmetric JWT signatures offline:

Step 1: Base64URL Decoding Helper

Standard atob() fails on URL-safe Base64 strings containing - and _. We convert them to standard Base64 with padding:

function base64UrlDecode(str: string): Uint8Array {
  let base64 = str.replace(/-/g, '+').replace(/_/g, '/');
  while (base64.length % 4) {
    base64 += '=';
  }
  const binary = atob(base64);
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(binary.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < binary.length; i++) {
    bytes[i] = binary.charCodeAt(i);
  }
  return bytes;
}

Step 2: Fetch and Match the Public Key from JWKS

We inspect the token header to locate the Key ID (kid) and find the corresponding public key in the identity provider's JWKS:

interface JwkKey {
  kty: string;
  kid: string;
  use: string;
  alg: string;
  n?: string;
  e?: string;
  crv?: string;
  x?: string;
  y?: string;
}

async function findJwkKey(jwksUrl: string, kid: string): Promise<JwkKey> {
  const response = await fetch(jwksUrl);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Failed to load JWKS: ${response.statusText}`);

  const data = await response.json();
  const matchedKey = data.keys.find((k: JwkKey) => k.kid === kid);

  if (!matchedKey) {
    throw new Error(`Public key with kid "${kid}" not found in JWKS.`);
  }
  return matchedKey;
}

Step 3: Import the JWK into the WebCrypto Runtime

We pass the raw JWK JSON directly into crypto.subtle.importKey():

async function importRsaPublicKey(jwk: JwkKey): Promise<CryptoKey> {
  return await window.crypto.subtle.importKey(
    "jwk",
    jwk,
    {
      name: "RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5",
      hash: { name: "SHA-256" }
    },
    false,       // Key is non-extractable
    ["verify"]   // Only authorized for verification
  );
}

(For ES256 ECDSA tokens, simply replace the algorithm name with { name: "ECDSA", namedCurve: "P-256" }).

Step 4: Mathematically Verify the Digital Signature

The cryptographic signature signs the UTF-8 ASCII representation of header.payload. We verify that signature against the imported public key:

async function verifyJwtSignature(rawJwt: string, cryptoKey: CryptoKey): Promise<boolean> {
  const parts = rawJwt.trim().split('.');
  if (parts.length !== 3) {
    throw new Error("Invalid JWT: Must contain header, payload, and signature segments.");
  }

  const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = parts;

  // The signed data is the ASCII string "header.payload"
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();
  const signedData = encoder.encode(`${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`);

  // Convert signature from Base64URL to raw bytes
  const signatureBytes = base64UrlDecode(signatureB64);

  // Execute mathematical hardware verification
  return await window.crypto.subtle.verify(
    "RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5",
    cryptoKey,
    signatureBytes,
    signedData
  );
}

If any character in the header or payload was modified, crypto.subtle.verify() returns false in less than two milliseconds.

Benchmark: In-Browser WebCrypto vs. Cloud Roundtrips

We benchmarked this client-side pipeline across 500 real-world RS256/ES256 tokens on Chrome 130 (macOS M2, 100 Mbps broadband):

Metric Traditional Cloud Decoder DevOmniTools In-Browser WebCrypto Delta
Average Latency 342.4 ms 1.8 ms 190x Faster
Data Sent to Wire 1,240 Bytes (Full Token + IP) 0.0 Bytes Zero Leakage
Offline Support ❌ Fails (HTTP 502) ✅ 100% Operational Seamless PWA
Replay Attack Risk ⚠️ High (Logged in caches) 🛡️ Zero (Never leaves RAM) Completely Immune
alg: none Defense ❌ Naively Accepted 🛡️ Blocked at Parser Strict Spec Enforcement

Visualizing Security States in the User Interface

To prevent engineers from mistaking a decoded payload for a verified token, we designed clear visual cryptographic states:

  • Green Badge (Signature Verified): Proves that the token was signed by the authentic private key matching the JWKS endpoint, and that not a single bit of the payload was altered in transit.
  • Red Badge (Signature Mismatch / Expired): Alerts the engineer immediately if the signature has been stripped, if the algorithm was downgraded, or if the token has expired past its exp claim.

What We Built & How to Use It

To solve this problem for ourselves and the engineering community, we integrated this complete zero-telemetry architecture into DevOmniTools:

👉 Try the Free In-Browser JWT Decoder & JWKS Verifier

  • 100% In-Browser Memory: All cryptographic hashing, Base64URL parsing, and JSON syntax formatting execute locally inside your browser tab.
  • Zero Server Uploads: Open your browser's Network tab and verify for yourself—zero bytes are transmitted over the wire when inspecting tokens.
  • Automatic JWKS Key Matching: Paste your token, provide your identity provider's JWKS endpoint or public key, and verify signatures in under 2 milliseconds.
  • Offline PWA Support: Installable as a Progressive Web App so you can inspect tokens on airplanes, disconnected VPNs, or air-gapped security enclaves.

4-Point Security Checklist for Your Team

Before you or your teammates paste another authentication token into a web tool, enforce these 4 safeguards:

  1. Check the Network Tab: Open Developer Tools before pasting a production token. If you see an HTTP POST request firing to a remote API, stop using that tool immediately.
  2. Never Paste Tokens with >1 Hour Lifetime: If you must use a third-party formatter, ensure the token is an expired test artifact, not a live production credential.
  3. Reject alg: none in Backend Code: Ensure your backend authentication middleware explicitly restricts permitted algorithms: 
   // Explicitly allow only RS256/ES256
   jwt.verify(token, getKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'] });
  1. Use In-Browser Verification: Adopt client-side cryptographic tools that leverage window.crypto.subtle to protect your team against accidental credential leaks.

What does your team use to debug OAuth tokens during local development? Have you audited the network traffic of your favorite developer utilities lately? Let's discuss in the comments below!
